articles.title: An Australian band’s ‘unreal’ journey to break a world record for most gigs in 12 hours
articles.summary: The dream rock band called Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia by car, helicopter and plane to play nine shows in 12 hours.
articles.body:
Dream rock band Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia to play nine shows, setting a new Guinness World Record for most concerts performed in 12 hours across multiple cities.

In order to beat the record, venues needed to be at least 50km apart in cities populated by more than 15,000 people, with half of the cities needing to have populations of at least 100,000.

Fathom partnered with a mental health service, Beyond Blue, donating half of the revenue from ticket sales and merchandise.

The BBC sat down with the duo to recount the day full of excitement and hurdles.

articles.title: Google expands its Android-based earthquake detection system
articles.summary: Google launched an earthquake early warning system for Android users last year, which it’s now rolling out in more locations.
articles.body: Google is expanding its Android-based earthquake detection and alert system, filling in gaps in places where there are few seismometers and no early warning systems. Starting today, the program that launched in California last year will also be available in Greece and New Zealand. This also marks a new step for Google; it’s the first time the company will handle everything from detecting the earthquake to warning individuals. Android devices will first sense waves generated by quakes. Google then analyzes data from the phones and sends out an early warning alert to users in the affected area. Users will get the alerts automatically unless they opt out of the service. When Google started on this endeavor, it worked with the United States Geological Survey and the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services to send earthquake alerts to Android users in California. This feature is now available in Oregon and will expand to Washington in May. Last year, Google started gathering earthquake data from phones. It then used that data to provide information to users if they searched for “earthquake” or “earthquake near me” on their phones. Google’s system works because each phone is already equipped with an accelerometer, which can detect movement. The accelerometer can also detect primary and secondary earthquake waves, almost acting as a “mini seismometer, joining millions of other Android phones out there to form the world’s largest earthquake detection network,” according to Google. Seismometers are devices that detect ground movement, like earthquakes. “It’d be great if there were just seismometer-based systems everywhere that could detect earthquakes,” Marc Stogaitis, principle Android software engineer at Google, told The Verge last year. Because of costs and maintenance, he says, “that’s not really practical and it’s unlikely to have global coverage.” There are some limitations to Google’s system. People closest to the quake probably won’t get much advance warning since they’ll be the first ones to detect the quake. But their phones will help give a heads-up to others farther away, giving them crucial time to take shelter. Android is the leading OS system for smartphones, so this service has a lot of room to grow. Eventually, Google could develop an API based on its earthquake detection system that could have farther-reaching effects. Other systems could use the API to let people off an elevator or open firehouse doors before losing power, Dieter Bohn wrote for The Verge last year. That’s still pretty far off but could make a huge difference in keeping people safe during future earthquakes.

articles.title: Marc Andreessen is a philosophical zombie
articles.summary: Andreessen caused a minor kerfuffle by saying on a podcast that he doesn’t introspect at all, and that in fact, people shouldn’t. What’s really going on?
articles.body: I admit, this is an innovation I did not see coming: Silicon Valley has invented the philosophical zombie from the classic thought experiment “lol how crazy would it be if there were a philosophical zombie.” Until recently, the philosophical zombie was a concept closely associated with Australian philosopher David Chalmers, who defines it as “someone or something physically identical to me (or to any other conscious being), but lacking conscious experiences altogether.” Chalmers’ zombie twin is identical to him functionally and psychologically — except that he feels nothing. This is different from a Hollywood zombie, which has “little capacity for introspection and lack[s] a refined ability to voluntarily control behavior.” So okay, Marc Andreessen is even shallower than our standard philosophical zombie — but still, I think there is a strong case he should be hunted and captured by the Stanford philosophy department so they can try their thought experiments out on him in real life. (Humanely, of course.) But I think for all of us who are interested in consciousness, Andreessen is certainly a specimen. [Media: For those of you who are not as internet-poisoned as I am, let me recap: A video of Andreessen on David Senra’s podcast — podcasts being Andreessen’s favored form of self-disclosure — has been making the rounds. In the video, Andreessen cheerfully says he has “zero” levels of introspection — “as little as possible.” This is a positive for entrepreneurs, we are told. “And you know, if you go back 400 years ago, it never would have occurred to anybody to be introspective,” Andreessen says, thus setting himself up for thunderous dunking. I could point to the many ancient traditions of introspection (set out variously in the Bhagavad Gita, Plato, or Psalm 119) or note that his comments about a “guilt-based whammy” that showed up from Vienna in the 1910s and 1920s due to the work of Sigmund Freud suggests Andreessen has never met a Catholic (and is unfamiliar with major Catholic thought, to boot, as introspection is famously important to St. Augustine). I could post a portrait of René “I think therefore I am” Descartes. I could note that this is such a significant misunderstanding of Freud as to suggest Andreessen is totally unfamiliar with him. I am not going to do any of those things, as I believe they have already been done by internet commenters. I am instead going to try to set out what happened, which is that I believe Andreessen read a book. The reference Andreessen gives is The Mind Is Flat by Nick Chater, a professor of behavioral science at the Warwick Business School at the University of Warwick in the UK. Now personally I am somewhat skeptical of how serious a book is when its title references Thomas Friedman, especially when it is being written by some business school guy. Still, the basic thrust of the book — as far as I can tell — is a polemic against the notion of an unconscious mind. I have not read the book, so I am relying on a lecture Chater gave at Google and reviews by his peers in order to summarize it; if this seems unfair to Andreessen, I am happy at his request to actually read the book and do this again in much more irritating detail. In Chater’s Google lecture, he begins by providing a series of optical illusions, demonstrating that our vision cannot work the way we believe it works. This is pretty convincing stuff! It turns out perception is very weird. (That noise you just heard was everyone who’s ever taken a philosophy 101 class yell “qualia” in unison. That’s the philosophy word for the “red-ness” of the color red, or the sensation of the smell of napalm in the morning.) From here, Chater proposes that the idea of an “inner self” is an illusion similar to the illusion we experience when we think we are perceiving more than one color at once. According to Chater, our minds can only do one thing at a time — that is, that we cannot have two thoughts at once, and the idea that we can is an illusion. From there, he suggests that there are no mental depths, there’s no such thing as the unconscious, and there’s no organizing principle to anyone’s mind. To the degree that an “inner self” exists, it is a kind of “tradition,” the cumulative effect of your accumulated experiences, just as a canyon exists because of the cumulative effects of water. There are some obvious problems with this polemic, which are highlighted in the reviews. The key thing I think Andreessen is badly summarizing is an assertion Chater makes in his Google speech: The idea that the conscious mind is like the part of the iceberg above water and that there is a mysterious part of the self below the water is attributable to Sigmund Freud, and this conception of the “larger self” is wrong. There’s only the part above the water. Here’s Andreessen’s read of Chater: “TLDR There is no inner self, you’re chasing an imaginary concept, the end.” In one of several follow-up posts to the interview on X, Andreessen went on to something even sillier: “You’re a 15 second sliding context window with the working memory of a goldfish, your long term memory is mainly fake, and it’s a minor miracle you can get out of the door in the morning.” It’s impressive in the sense that almost every single part of Andreessen’s sentence is wrong. I will begin, pedantically, with the goldfish, which actually have impressive memories, like, years’ worth. But let’s get to the point: “your long term memory is mainly fake.” I suppose this depends on what Andreessen means, doesn’t it? On the one hand, any cradle Catholic can do an “Our Father” or a “Hail Mary” basically at will for the rest of their lives, even if they haven’t set foot in a church in 20 years. There are other indications that memory is in some sense “real”: Small studies suggest that musical memory is preserved even in Alzheimer’s patients. Finally, most of us have attended a play, where actors recite speeches at will. How this is possible if long-term memory is fake, I don’t know. On the other hand, long-term memory can be unreliable — it is possible even to implant false memories. But “mainly fake”? I hope Andreessen stretched before that reach. Obviously, if you’re a “sliding 15 second context window” it would be impossible to have consistent thoughts, preferences, and beliefs over time — except, of course, people do. Personality may change over a lifetime, but there is often stability for years or decades. As for “it’s a minor miracle you can get out of bed in the morning,” well, I have to assume this reflects Andreessen’s own mornings. (Also, any parent of a toddler can tell you that gross motor skills are independent of sophisticated thought, memory, or introspection.) This is the only part of the sentence I can’t really argue with — I personally don’t have much trouble getting out of bed, but I can’t speak for him. At this point, a reader may be tempted to point out to me that Andreessen is trolling, and I am taking him far too seriously. But unfortunately for everyone, Andreessen has waded into an interest of mine, making it intersect with my actual job. He has been posting about his theory of mind for days now — a repeated behavior, which suggests it must be important to him. So since we’re doing quasi-scientific polemics, I’ll throw my own in. I’ve been wondering for a while why many of our Silicon Valley overlords behave like they’ve repeatedly sustained traumatic brain injuries, and I think I’ve come to a conclusion. One thing we know from a variety of studies is that cognition doesn’t decline for some people as they age — those people tend to have stayed in school longer and tend to have greater intellectual engagement. We also know that if you don’t use one of your languages on a regular basis, you start to forget it — even if it was your first language. Writing by hand is better for memory; predictive text leads to boring writing. I am now going to extrapolate from this: If you stop using some skill, mental or physical, you lose it and its benefits. We’ve already seen signs of this with heavy users of AI, along with AI psychosis, which may occur because chatbots are too sycophantic. (I have pitched my editors on attempting to give myself AI psychosis, but they seem to think I am making a joke.) So I’m going to suggest that overreliance on AI is bad for you — which suggests a corollary: Whatever is happening to normal people as a result of AI overreliance has already happened to the ultra-wealthy. Consider: I spend a lot of time standing in line (at the supermarket, at the post office, at a bakery, at a coffee shop). While I’m standing there, I can either be annoyed at how long it’s taking me to get to the front of the line or do something else: goof around on social media or retreat into my mind palace, where I might daydream, review events from earlier in the day, or think about something interesting, like whether it matters if I don’t have free will. I have a lot of opportunities to hang out in my mind palace, because I do a lot of mundane chores, like grocery shopping, laundry, and picking up after myself. The ultra-wealthy don’t have to do any of this. They pay people to do it for them — cooking, cleaning, shopping, you name it. There are no periods of the day where they are forced to figure out how to entertain themselves in the face of repetitive chores. If you don’t use it, you lose it — so maybe a lot of them lose introspection. In fact, they can offload any cognitive activity they don’t enjoy! That’s what subordinates are for, isn’t it? And whatever gets consistently offloaded, they lose. But, worse, they don’t notice they’re losing any skills because they are constantly surrounded by people on their payroll, or people who want something from them. People who are, you know, aggressively financially motivated to flatter them and agree with them. If that yes-man tendency in chatbots is what’s driving AI psychosis or social skill atrophy in normal people, then the same thing has already happened to the very rich. So I am inclined to take Andreessen at his word. He’s having a little meltdown, as he sometimes does, first of all because people are making fun of him online — a thing he doesn’t encounter on a regular basis outside social media due to the yes-man phenomenon of wealth, and which is for this reason much more upsetting for him than it would be to a normal person. He has wholesale adopted Chater’s thinking, or at least a version of it, and it probably felt revelatory and correct to him because his own mind is shallow. (He doesn’t strike me as the kind of guy who’s thought about the hard problem of consciousness much, you know?) I’m not convinced he knows he was reading a polemic. But second, I also believe him when he says he doesn’t introspect. Because we know he agrees with Chater, we can just use Chater’s definition of thought here, bracketing whatever problems that definition may have. Because introspection under Chater’s definition is just another kind of perception, Andreessen has just functionally told us that he is missing qualia. We’ve got ourselves a philosophical zombie right here, and possibly a methodology for creating them at will. Someone should get on the horn to Australia — Chalmers is going to be so excited. I am also going to presume that in his posts, Andreessen is describing himself. But obviously there’s some overlap with a thing that Andreessen invests in, which is to say AI — which also has no long-term memory, no actual perception (and no qualia), and no ability to get out of bed. It is possible that Andreessen likes Chater because Chater suggests there is no depth to humans, which means that AI “intelligence” is very close to human intelligence, which means AI can replace humans at their jobs and Andreessen’s investments will make a boatload more money. So, inspired by Vanity Fair, I thought it might be fun to interview Andreessen via ChatGPT — an a16z investment — since he seems to be implying that humans aren’t much different than AI. (Andreessen’s firm is also invested in xAI, but I think asking Mecha Hitler to impersonate Andreessen is probably too rude, even for me.) I asked ChatGPT, roleplaying as Andreessen, why he didn’t introspect; it told me “I wouldn’t actually say that,” before going on at length about why people who want to be entrepreneurs should use it but also “validate everything against external feedback.” But hey, if improvising nonsense is all Andreessen does, this is as much of an answer as the real guy can give us. So I decided to ask ChatGPTeessen another question: What did Andreessen mean when he wrote “Introspection = neuroticism x narcissism x thumbsucking”? Here’s the answer: --- What I meant is: most of what people call “introspection” is not some high-fidelity path to truth—it’s a distortion loop. Break it down. * Neuroticism: you’re obsessing over your own thoughts, replaying decisions, second-guessing. That’s not clarity—that’s anxiety masquerading as insight. * Narcissism: you’re assuming your internal state is uniquely important, that your feelings are the central object worth analyzing. In reality, the world doesn’t care. Markets don’t care. Users don’t care. * Thumbsucking: you’re not acting. You’re sitting there, self-soothing with analysis instead of making decisions and moving forward. So the equation is deliberately provocative, but the point is practical: introspection is often a trap. In startups, this kills you. Founders sit around debating their own motivations, their fears, their identity—meanwhile someone else is shipping product, talking to customers, and taking the market. The bias should be toward external reality and action: * What do users do, not what do you feel * What works, not what you think should work * What ships, not what you’ve analyzed Use introspection sparingly, like a diagnostic tool. But if it becomes your default mode, you’re just spinning in place. --- This answer, much like the first one, doesn’t sound stylistically like Andreessen: It’s not succinct or tendentious enough. On the other hand, it’s an improvising 15-second context window with no introspection telling me what Marc Andreessen thinks, which is what Andreessen also claims to be. And the gist does sound like his thinking, doesn’t it? If there’s no “inner self,” what’s the difference? So I guess we’ve all learned something important: Marc Andreessen, a philosophical zombie, can be easily replaced with AI. I bet that’s great news for a16z’s investors, since it means Andreessen no longer must be paid — and it frees him up to be the subject of some philosophy experiments. (Well, unless the neuroscientists get to him first, I guess.) I look forward to finding out what it’s like to be a philosophical zombie — or maybe that it’s not like anything to be a philosophical zombie.

articles.title: Wolves and foxes may be helping plants spread across the Sahara Desert; scientists found seeds from eight species in their droppings
articles.summary: Deep in the Sahara Desert, where rain is rare and plants struggle to spread, an unlikely desert gardener may be at work.
articles.body: Deep in the Sahara Desert, where rain is rare and plants struggle to spread, an unlikely desert gardener may be at work. Researchers who sifted through hundreds of carnivore droppings found intact seeds from eight different plant species, suggesting that wolves and foxes may help desert vegetation spread across the landscape. If you have ever wondered how shrubs and palms reach new ground in such harsh country, the answer may be hiding in what predators leave behind. This article explains what scientists discovered, which animals favoured which fruits, and why those scattered seeds could matter for the fragile desert ecosystems.How scientists searched 597 carnivore dropping samples in the Sahara Desert for hidden plant seedsA research team including Inmaculada Cancio, José María Gil-Sánchez, Emilio Virgós and others set out to learn whether meat-eating mammals can move plant seeds across one of the most significant hyper-arid regions on Earth. Their 2026 study ‘Seed dispersal by carnivores in a hyper-arid habitat: insights from the Sahara Desert’ in the Journal of Arid Environments, which the authors present as the first evidence of its kind for the Sahara Desert, notes that other animals able to carry seeds are scarce there. The scientists collected 597 faecal samples from four carnivores, the North African golden wolf, the red fox, Rüppell's fox and the honey badger. They measured how often seeds appeared in droppings, compared the fruits animals ate with the fruits actually available, and counted the undamaged seeds, contrasting optimal and less suitable habitat for germination.Eight desert plant species found in droppings, including Ziziphus lotus, date palm and Ephedra alataSeeds from eight plant species turned up, Ziziphus lotus, Lycium shawii, Asparagus altissimus, Searsia tripartita, Nitraria retusa, the date palm Phoenix dactylifera, Ephedra alata and Balanites aegyptiaca. They came from three canids, meaning members of the dog family, and one mustelid, the honey badger, a member of the weasel family. According to the authors, the frequency of occurrence of seeds in droppings ranged from 9.47 per cent to 35.29 per cent for each species and study period. In samples that contained seeds, the researchers found an average of 12.9 intact seeds per dropping, with a margin of error of 2.4. Intact seeds matter because a crushed seed rarely becomes a plant, whereas seeds that pass through the digestive tract with minimal damage may keep their ability to grow.Why wolves favour one desert fruit while foxes choose berries from other shrubs in the Sahara DesertWolves and foxes showed different tastes. Wolves preferentially consumed the drupes of Ziziphus lotus, fleshy fruits with a hard stone inside, while foxes selected the berries of Lycium shawii and Asparagus altissimus. Because the team compared the fruits animals ate with those actually available, the pattern reflects selection rather than simple abundance. These animals are well suited to the job. The authors explain that carnivores can eat a wide variety of fruit sizes and types, and that canids and mustelids take fruit that has already fallen to the ground. Their large spatial requirements also make carnivores especially important as long-distance seed carriers, which can connect plant populations and help new areas become colonized. For a desert plant, that kind of reach could be invaluable.Why seeds left in dry riverbeds and ravines could help desert vegetation take hold across the SaharaThe most striking result concerns where the seeds end up. Of the intact seeds found in droppings, 72.4 percent were deposited in habitats the team considered optimal for germination, namely dry riverbeds and secondary ravines, amounting to 1,038.9 undamaged seeds per square kilometer, with a margin of 351.1. That matters because the authors note that where seeds land often shapes dispersal quality more than how far or how many they travel. Based on these findings, they conclude that canids play an important role as seed dispersers in the Sahara Desert, and they suggest similar animal and plant partnerships could be relevant across other hyper-arid areas. With the Sahara described as one of the most poorly preserved ecoregions on Earth, the authors argue that studies like theirs are essential for its conservation.

articles.title: Hippos transfer 0.4 tonnes of silicon into Kenya’s Mara River on a dry-season day; scientists explain why the element matters to aquatic life
articles.summary: Hippos spend their nights grazing on grass and their days resting in rivers.
articles.body: Hippos spend their nights grazing on grass and their days resting in rivers. This daily routine also moves silicon from land into water, where it can influence the organisms that form the base of aquatic food webs. In a study published in Science Advances titled Hippos (Hippopotamus amphibius): The animal silicon pump, researchers estimated that hippos transfer 0.4 metric tonnes of silicon into Kenya’s Mara River on a dry-season day by eating grass on land and depositing dung in the water. Their model estimated that hippos influence up to 76% of silicon flux along the study reach in the Maasai Mara. These estimates came from a dry-season study of one river, not a global assessment. The findings nevertheless show how large animals can connect terrestrial ecosystems with rivers and potentially affect aquatic food webs downstream.Hippo silicon pump explained: how grazing and dung move silicon into the Mara RiverThe researchers conducted their field sampling in February 2014 along the Mara River in south-western Kenya, where hippos graze on savannah grasslands at night and congregate in river pools during the day. Silicon absorbed by grasses can pass through the animals’ digestive systems and enter the river through their dung, bypassing some of the processes that would otherwise retain silicon in the soil. The researchers measured biogenic silicon, a form of silicon produced by living organisms, in grass and hippo dung. Grass in the Maasai Mara National Reserve contained an average of 1.8% biogenic silicon by dry weight, while hippo dung contained 4.1%. Using earlier estimates from a 2015 study, ‘The hippopotamus conveyor belt’, that hippos consume 42.0 metric tonnes of dry grass and deposit 11.1 metric tonnes of dry dung in the river each day, the researchers estimated a daily transfer of approximately 0.4 metric tonnes of silicon. At the time of sampling, the Mara River carried daily fluxes of 7.9 metric tonnes of dissolved silicon and 2.4 metric tonnes of biogenic silicon. The researchers estimated that hippos directly accounted for 32% of the increase in biogenic silicon flux between the most upstream and most downstream sampling sites. They attributed the remaining increase partly to resuspended riverbed material, which can contain silicon from older hippo dung, as well as dust and indirect inputs such as faeces deposited on riverbanks. Some of these additional sources may also be linked to hippos.Monitoring over 24 hours along a 250-metre stretch of river where up to 80 hippos were present also showed that biogenic silicon concentrations doubled relative to upstream values. Laboratory experiments found that 2.8% of the biogenic silicon in fresh hippo dung dissolved after 24 hours in rainwater. This was 17.2 times the proportion released from undigested grass under the study’s experimental conditions. The researchers used a mass-balance model to estimate the contribution of hippos to silicon flux along the study reach in the Maasai Mara. Their calculation suggested that hippos influenced up to 76% of the flux, but this estimate depended on a model assumption that the sediment contained an effectively unlimited stock of biogenic silicon. The authors acknowledged that sedimentation and resuspension vary, making the real system more complex. They also cautioned that the estimate came from dry-season observations and could overstate the contribution of hippos under other seasonal conditions.Silicon, diatoms and aquatic food webs: why river inputs matterSilicon is important to diatoms, microscopic algae that use dissolved silicon to build their glass-like cell walls. Diatoms contribute substantially to aquatic primary production and support food webs by providing food for other organisms. The availability of silicon can therefore influence the composition of phytoplankton communities. The Science Advances researchers explain that a reduction in riverine silicon supply could change the balance between diatoms and other algae, with potential consequences for aquatic food webs. Their study considered the possible implications for Lake Victoria and other East African lakes, where river inputs contribute to silicon availability.The Mara River contributes about 5% of the water flowing into Lake Victoria, according to the study. However, the researchers did not directly measure how the silicon transferred by hippos affects the lake’s algal communities or food web. The downstream consequences remain a potential implication of their findings rather than a demonstrated outcome. A press release from the GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences, whose researchers contributed to the study, explains that insufficient silicon can disadvantage diatoms relative to other algae. Some algal blooms can contribute to oxygen depletion and fish deaths, creating problems for aquatic ecosystems and communities that depend on fishing. These are possible consequences of changes in silicon availability, not effects that the hippo study directly established in Lake Victoria.Hippo dung benefits and risks: how large animals can also affect river oxygen levelsHippos transport more than silicon from grasslands into rivers. In a separate study, The hippopotamus conveyor belt, researchers examined how hippos move organic matter and nutrients from terrestrial habitats into aquatic systems. These inputs can provide resources for aquatic organisms, but excessive organic matter can also affect water quality. A 2018 study published in Nature Communications, titled Organic matter loading by hippopotami causes subsidy overload resulting in downstream hypoxia and fish kills, documented repeated low-oxygen events in the Mara River. Researchers recorded 49 high-flow events associated with decreases in dissolved oxygen over three years. Thirteen of these events resulted in hypoxia, or critically low oxygen levels, and the researchers documented nine fish kills over five years. Experiments and modelling linked the oxygen depletion to high flows that flush oxygen-depleted water and organic matter from hippo pools into downstream sections of the river. As this material decomposes, it can consume oxygen faster than flowing water replenishes it. The researchers suggested that similar events may have been more widespread in Africa before hippo populations declined, although this historical possibility was not directly measured.

articles.title: Nasa heated a yoga-ball-sized Venus probe model to 869°F in a Pennsylvania furnace, running the test 6 times
articles.summary: Nasa engineers have tested whether an engineering model of the DAVINCI Venus descent probe can protect its scientific instruments from the extreme heat it
articles.body: Nasa engineers have tested whether an engineering model of the DAVINCI Venus descent probe can protect its scientific instruments from the extreme heat it will encounter while travelling through the planet’s atmosphere. The model, roughly the size of a yoga ball, was placed in a furnace at Rex Heat Treat in Bedford, Pennsylvania, and heated to 869°F (465°C) over about 1 hour. The team repeated the thermal cycle 5 more times, and the model emerged from all 6 runs without damage, according to NASA Science. Conducted from Aug. 28 to Sept. 10, 2026, the test assessed the probe’s ability to insulate its internal instruments as the outside heats rapidly during descent. The results are an important engineering milestone, although the test does not by itself establish that the complete flight spacecraft is ready for launch.Nasa’s DAVINCI probe heat test: 869°F in a Pennsylvania furnaceThe test took place at Rex Heat Treat in Bedford, Pennsylvania. Nasa selected the facility because it is among the few capable of raising hardware to Venus-like temperatures at a rate comparable to the heating the probe will experience during its descent. Engineers placed the engineering model inside a ceramic-lined furnace chamber and raised the temperature to 869°F (465°C) over approximately 1 hour. They then repeated the thermal cycle 5 times, producing 6 runs in total. The model remained intact throughout the tests.More than 100 thermal sensors monitored hardware simulating the probe’s internal science instruments. These measurements allowed engineers to assess how effectively the probe’s outer structure would shield the instruments from the rising temperature. Jim Garvin, DAVINCI’s principal investigator at Nasa’s Goddard Space Flight Center, described the experiment as a successful series of 6 runs following the mission’s planned 55-to-60-minute descent timeline, with the internal instrumentation represented in the test setup. He also said that the United States had not conducted such a complete assessment of spacecraft-scale hardware at Venus temperatures since the mid-1970s. The test showed that the engineering model survived the six thermal cycles while protecting hardware simulating the probe’s instruments. They do not mean that every part of the eventual flight probe has completed qualification or that the spacecraft has already received approval for its next development phase.DAVINCI probe design: titanium shell, thermal protection and gas-inlet portsThe probe must protect its instruments while allowing them to sample Venus’s atmosphere. These requirements create a difficult engineering problem: the vessel needs to limit heat transfer to its internal hardware, but it must also admit atmospheric gases for scientific analysis. Nasa says the probe is enclosed in a corrosion-resistant titanium shell designed to be strong yet lightweight. Special inlet ports will allow atmospheric gases to enter so that the instruments can measure their composition. The recent furnace test focused on the model’s ability to manage the thermal environment, rather than demonstrating every aspect of the probe’s scientific operation. During its descent, DAVINCI’s instruments are intended to examine the composition and structure of Venus’s atmosphere. The mission will measure atmospheric properties and sample gases to investigate how the planet formed and evolved.The probe will also carry cameras designed to capture close-up images of a mountainous region called Alpha Regio. Nasa says these observations are intended to provide detailed views of the terrain and help scientists build a 3D understanding of the surface. A spacecraft flying above the descent probe will receive the data for transmission back to Earth. The planned descent will last roughly an hour. The thermal test therefore addresses a critical design requirement: the probe must preserve its instruments long enough to collect measurements in an environment far hotter than conditions on Earth.DAVINCI mission to Venus: helicopter imaging tests and the search for the planet’s pastThe furnace experiment is one part of DAVINCI’s wider development programme. The mission is designed to investigate how Venus’s atmosphere formed and evolved, including whether the planet may once have had liquid-water oceans and conditions more favourable to life. Although Venus is similar to Earth in size, its present-day environment is dramatically different. Its dense atmosphere produces an extreme greenhouse effect, making it the hottest planet in the solar system. Measurements from DAVINCI could help researchers understand how the two planets developed along different evolutionary paths.In July 2026, Nasa reported another preparation milestone: helicopter flights over Crater Island in Utah tested a prototype of the probe’s imaging system. During the campaign, the helicopter carried a basket containing 9 instruments, including infrared cameras and sensors. The flights simulated a near-vertical descent, allowing researchers to test whether images from the camera system could be used to reconstruct terrain and identify rock types. The resulting maps were compared with existing geological and topographic maps. The imaging campaign and the thermal tests address different technical challenges. The Utah flights evaluated the approach to collecting and interpreting descent images, while the Pennsylvania furnace runs tested the engineering model’s ability to protect simulated instruments from intense heat.Nasa says DAVINCI is working towards approval to enter the final design and fabrication phase. The successful furnace test is therefore a significant step in evaluating the probe’s design, but it is not evidence that the mission has already entered that phase. By combining atmospheric measurements with detailed images of Alpha Regio, DAVINCI aims to provide new information about Venus’s chemistry, surface and history. The recent tests help engineers assess whether the probe’s systems can withstand the conditions required to gather that information.

articles.title: NASA's latest satellite imagery reveals Australia's giant spider; the striking landscape created by an ancient impact is a huge crater
articles.summary: From the ground it may look like just another isolated patch of tough Australian country.
articles.body: From the ground it may look like just another isolated patch of tough Australian country. From space, however, the landscape takes on an uncanny form: a giant spider etched across the earth. Spider Crater, hidden away in Western Australia’s Kimberley region, isn’t just the work of nature’s more familiar forces. It has a strange shape, created by a meteor strike hundreds of millions of years ago. A recent satellite image has brought the amazing formation into sharp focus, revealing how closely its central pattern resembles the creature that gave it its name.A crater etched by the fury of the cosmosAccording to NASA, the Operational Land Imager on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite acquired the image on September 20, 2026. Seen from above, the whole impact structure is distinctly oval-shaped, measuring about 13 km by 11 km. At its heart is the feature that gives Spider Crater its disquieting look: a pattern of ridges about four kilometers wide radiating outwards like legs.The formation is believed to be the remnants of a central uplift, a raised section of the crater floor that occurs when the ground bounces back after the massive force of an impact. It started as a violent collision with an alien body, and over a long period, geological processes gradually shaped it.NASA says some of the more durable remnants of the original landscape are the pale sandstone ridges that make up the spiderlike pattern. Over time, the surrounding rock layers weathered and eroded away, leaving these more resistant formations behind, and exposing the unusual structure we see today.The volcanic enigma of impact cratersSpider Crater did not immediately give away its origins to scientists, according to NASA. There has been 40 years of debate over its strange shape, with competing ideas including the idea that volcanic eruptions created the formation, the NASA report says.As geologists began to study the rocks in the field more closely, that theory began to fade. Key among the clues were shatter cones, unique fan-shaped fractures that form when powerful shock waves move through rock. These structures are closely related to meteorite impacts and were seen all over the central dome of Spider Crater, the NASA report adds.More evidence came from lab studies of shocked quartz and zircon crystals found in the sandstone. According to the report, such minerals can record microscopic evidence of the tremendous pressures created during an impact and give hints about how the collision took place.A peek into Earth’s distant pastThe exact age of Spider Crater is unknown, but geologic evidence in the region surrounding the impact suggests an age between about 900 million and 600 million years ago. This makes the crater a relic of the late Precambrian, long before dinosaurs, flowering plants, or even complex life were familiar features of Earth's landscape. Over hundreds of millions of years erosion slowly peeled back layers of rock, leaving behind an old impact scar as the striking spider-shaped formation seen from above. NASA’s satellite images today provide a rare look at this geological survivor. Seen from orbit it looks almost playful, but it is in fact the beautifully preserved record of one of the most violent encounters Earth has ever had with space.Image Courtesy: NASA

articles.title: Northwestern scientists studying proteins linked to Alzheimer's found a single spot that helps harmful tau clumps spread; blocking that hotspot with a chemical tag stopped the clumps from growing in lab tests
articles.summary: Buried deep in the brain, a protein that normally helps sustain nerve cells can be a source of trouble.
articles.body: Buried deep in the brain, a protein that normally helps sustain nerve cells can be a source of trouble. When tau proteins change from their normal shape, they can start to cling together, creating tangled structures linked to Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia, an online report from Northwestern University says. Scientists have long grappled with the question of how these misshapen proteins can persuade healthy ones to do the same. Now, researchers at Northwestern University may have discovered a key vulnerability in that process, a single molecular hotspot that could offer a new target for future treatments.Finding the trigger for tau clumpingThe study was conducted by scientists at Northwestern University in collaboration with colleagues at the University of California, Santa Barbara, who investigated the misfolding of tau proteins and their assembly into long, threadlike structures called fibrils. The research, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, identified that there is a particular region of tau that seems to dominate in triggering the process.Normally, tau proteins are flexible and have no fixed structure. But if they misfold they can latch onto existing fibrils and adopt the same abnormal shape. As more proteins attach to the growing structure, the fibrils become longer and may help create neurofibrillary tangles within neurons. Such deposits are characteristic of several neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia. They can interfere with communication between nerve cells and contribute to the damage that occurs with cognitive decline.The surprising role of waterThe researchers found that the hotspot is in a hydrophobic part of tau — one that doesn't readily interact with water. But proteins are in a watery cellular environment, so these regions still need to be protected from their surroundings. The water molecules form a protective layer or cap around the hotspot, but it is a dynamic layer. Researchers found that these water structures help determine where two tau proteins come together.When hotspots come together, the water around them is released. The energy released by this process stabilizes the interaction, allowing the incoming tau protein to align with an existing fibril and assume its misfolded shape. The report found that tau proteins stack in a uniform order to allow for continued growth of the fibrils. The newly identified hotspot appears to help coordinate that process, offering a molecular explanation for how an initially disordered protein can build an orderly, expanding structure.When the hotspot is blocked, growth stopsTo determine whether the hotspot was important, the team attached a chemical tag to the region they had found. In laboratory experiments, this intervention blocked the growth of tau fibrils. The researchers also identified two other areas, away from the hotspot. These interventions did not stop fibril growth, adding weight to the idea that the site identified plays a particularly important role in the process.Thus, disrupting this interaction could eventually be a way to stop misfolded tau from dragging other proteins along. But the experiments were conducted in the lab, and more research will be needed to determine if the approach can be safely and effectively used in living organisms.A shortcut for future therapies perhapsIf a specific molecular target can be identified, researchers can hone in on potential treatments, rather than trying to block tau aggregation across the entire protein. The discovery could also lead to the development of diagnostic tools and synthetic tau fibrils that more accurately mimic disease-related structures for laboratory research.Scientists have struggled to create dependable models of these rogue proteins, making it difficult for them to study how various tau-related diseases progress and to test possible treatments.The Northwestern-led study shows how a specific region helps misfolded tau propagate, identifying a more precise starting point for future studies. The discovery is not a treatment for Alzheimer’s, yet, but it finds a potential weakness in one of the molecular processes associated with neurodegeneration, a small target that could have widespread implications for research into diseases that remain difficult to treat.Images Courtesy: istock

articles.title: Christina Koch named Nasa’s acting deputy chief engineer after Artemis II; appointment ends her eligibility for future spaceflights
articles.summary: A veteran astronaut who has lived in orbit for nearly a year and flown around the Moon is now moving from the cockpit to the engineering leadership table.
articles.body: A veteran astronaut who has lived in orbit for nearly a year and flown around the Moon is now moving from the cockpit to the engineering leadership table. Christina Koch, an electrical engineer by training, will serve as acting deputy chief engineer at the Nasa from November 1. The appointment ends her eligibility for future spaceflight, yet it also places her at the center of decisions about technical standards, mission readiness and engineering excellence. Here is what the announcement means, whom Koch is succeeding, what agency leaders are saying, and why her North Carolina roots matter.Christina Koch becomes acting deputy chief engineer on November 1 after Katherine Van Hooser retiresAccording to the official news release the Nasa on October 13, Christina Koch will begin serving as acting deputy chief engineer on Sunday, November 1. The post opens because Katherine Van Hooser, the agency's deputy chief engineer since 2023, retires on Wednesday, October 21, after more than 35 years of service. In her new role, Koch will help lead the agency's engineering community, supporting technical oversight, mission readiness and engineering excellence across programs and projects. The release confirms that she will move to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments. WRAL adds that her responsibilities will cover both crewed and robotic missions, including engineering standards and technical reviews.What agency chiefs say Koch brings to engineering oversight, technical reviews and mission readinessAgency leaders have been direct about why they chose her. Administrator Jared Isaacman told readers of the official news release that Koch has seen engineering from "both sides of the equation," building complex systems on the ground and trusting them with her life in space. He added that her nearly year-long stay aboard the International Space Station and her role in Artemis II give her technical expertise, operational experience and sound judgment. Isaacman also linked the appointment to the agency's goals of returning Americans to the lunar surface, building the Moon Base, advancing nuclear power in space and eventually reaching Mars.From Goddard Space Flight Center engineer to record-setting astronaut and Artemis II specialist roleKoch's path began in engineering rather than in the astronaut corps. The official news release explains that she started as an electrical engineer at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, developing scientific instruments for space missions, and also worked as a scientific field engineer in Antarctica and the Arctic before her selection as an astronaut in 2013. WRAL's Tony Rice reports that she later contributed to instruments for the Juno spacecraft and the Van Allen Probes at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. In space, she spent 328 consecutive days aboard the International Space Station, the longest single spaceflight by a woman, and took part in the first all-female spacewalks with fellow astronaut Jessica Meir. In April, she served as a mission specialist on Artemis II.North Carolina State University roots: Three degrees, a mural and the Koch Hall dedication in AugustKoch's story is also a North Carolina story. WRAL reports that she earned two bachelor's degrees in 2001, in electrical engineering and physics, and a master's degree in electrical engineering in 2002, all from North Carolina State University. That makes her a three-time graduate of the institution. In August 2026, the university dedicated its Engineering Building II as Koch Hall, honoring her as an engineer, explorer and astronaut. The building houses the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, where her academic journey began, and a mural of Koch now appears in the campus free expression tunnel. For students in Raleigh and beyond, her rise from classroom to Moon mission shows how engineering education can lead directly to human exploration.Katherine Van Hooser's legacy and the engineering challenges Koch inherits as the Moon Base advancesKoch steps into a role shaped by a long career. The official news release notes that Van Hooser joined the agency in 1991 at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, worked on liquid rocket engine turbomachinery, and became chief engineer for the space shuttle main engine through the final 21 shuttle flights. She later served as the first chief engineer of the Space Launch System Liquid Engines Element. Amit Kshatriya, associate administrator and chief engineer, said via the release that he is grateful for her exceptional service and confident Koch will continue the tradition of technical excellence essential to everything the agency does. Koch now inherits that standard as lunar landings, the Moon Base and nuclear power in space move forward.

articles.title: Ukraine claims Starlink is suddenly disrupting service for its military
articles.summary: Ukrainian officials claim Elon Musk’s Starlink imposed new restrictions on service in the area, disrupting its drone operations and missions.
articles.body: Ukrainian officials claim the Elon Musk-owned Starlink put new limits on its service in the area without warning, disrupting the country’s drone operations and missions, according to reports from Reuters and the Financial Times. The move comes just days after Musk wrote on X that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy “has gone too far,” in response to President Donald Trump’s disapproval of Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries. “It is clear that this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation,” Ukrainian defense tech advisor Serhii Beskrestnov writes on Telegram. Earlier this week, Russia launched a barrage of missiles that struck multiple power plants in Ukraine, despite the “energy ceasefire” Trump claimed that the two countries have reached. Zelenskyy said in a post on X that the military received “no advance warning from our partners about the ballistic missile launch.” Beskrestnov writes that Starlink has imposed a new restriction that prevents it from connecting to devices traveling at over 100mph. He adds that this has “led to the disruption of several missions,” as reported by Reuters. The limitation is impacting Ukraine’s ability to protect itself from Russian drone strikes as well, Beskrestnov says. The apparent Starlink restriction has begun to draw criticism from international leaders. Radosław Sikorski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, which pays for Ukraine’s Starlink subscription, issued a warning to Musk on X: “Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you.” SpaceX didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

articles.title: The first new sunscreen type in 25 years has arrived on US store shelves
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — For the first time in more than a quarter-century, Americans have a new option when shopping for sunscreen: a skin-protecting chemical that...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — For the first time in more than a quarter-century, Americans have a new option when shopping for sunscreen: a skin-protecting chemical that's long been a go-to option in Europe and other parts of the world.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved bemotrizinol — sometimes called BEMT — in June. The first sunscreens containing it are now hitting U.S. store shelves, including formulas from Neutrogena and other manufacturers.

Dermatologists say the chemical fills an important market gap by offering broad protection, like the most well-established sunscreen ingredients, but without their cosmetic downsides, including white streaking .

BEMT has decades of safety data behind it, including studies showing it has minimal absorption into the skin. That's been a concern with some older sun-blocking chemicals.

"It's not a brand-new ingredient that you're going to be the first person to try," said Dr. Jennifer Stein, a dermatologist at NYU Langone Health.

New ingredient offers broad protection without streaks

To be effective, sunscreens must protect against both forms of ultraviolet light that can damage the skin — UVB rays, which cause most sunburn, and UVA rays that pose the greatest risk of skin cancer and wrinkles .

Sunscreens that block both forms are labeled "broad spectrum protection." Those that don't must carry an FDA warning label.

BEMT is the first chemical-based sunscreen in the U.S. that offers this dual protection. Previously, manufacturers had to mix multiple ingredients to protect against both UVA and UVB light.

"This ingredient provides a solution for what is currently a big gap with respect to providing strong UVA protection," said David Andrews, chief science officer of the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit that advocates for higher sunscreen standards .

A different class of sunscreens, using minerals such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, has long been shown to offer strong protection against both forms of ultraviolet light. These mineral-based formulas work by physically blocking harmful rays from the skin.

But some people — particularly those with darker complexions — tend to avoid them because they cause white streaking and discoloration. In other cases, people don't like their texture or consistency.

"Those are good sunscreens," Stein said. "But for people who aren't so inclined to use them — maybe they don't like how it feels on their skin — this is a nice option."

There's less skin penetration with the new formula

The fact that chemical-based sunscreens are absorbed into the skin means they have to be carefully studied to make sure they aren't building up in the body at unsafe levels.

Last month, the FDA revoked approval of an older chemical ingredient, oxybenzone, after determining it was "absorbed through the skin to a greater extent than previously understood."

"It's a molecule that's too big to really penetrate through the skin and get absorbed into the bloodstream," Stein said. "The older chemical sunscreens had small molecules."

As part of its safety review, the FDA reviewed studies of BEMT in more than 500 patients conducted by Dutch manufacturer DSM Nutritional Products. Levels of the chemical absorbed into the skin were nearly undetectable, the studies found.

Agency reviewers said research in people who used the sunscreen daily for up to three weeks showed that BEMT "did not cause irritation" or allergic reactions. As a result, the FDA designated the ingredient as "generally recognized as safe and effective," alongside the older mineral ingredients zinc oxide and titanium dioxide.

More than a dozen other ingredients are currently used in U.S. sunscreens, but the FDA has said they will require additional evidence to support their safety and effectiveness. The FDA review is part of an ongoing effort to overhaul U.S. sunscreen ingredients that kicked off in 2019.

More evidence is needed about the impact on coral reefs

Scientists have shown that some sunscreen ingredients can trigger bleaching and damage coral reefs . That's led to bans on two chemical ingredients — oxybenzone, the ingredient recently targeted by the FDA, and octinoxate — in Hawaii and parts of Florida. It's estimated about 25% of the sunscreen people apply to their skin washes off while swimming or wading in the ocean.

The U.S. government doesn't classify the environmental impact of sunscreens, and marketing claims like "reef safe" or "reef friendly" have no standard definition or requirements. The European Union's environmental agency has found "limited evidence of environmental toxicity" with BEMT, but longer-term research is needed.

Mineral ingredients like zinc oxide are generally considered safer for the environment, although some experts recommend staying away from so-called nano formulations. Those products are made with tiny particles that are more likely to be inhaled or absorbed by marine organisms.

Experts say BEMT has one other key advantage, in that it doesn't quickly break down in the sun. That's been a particular issue for avobenzone, the only other chemical-based ingredient that filters UVA light.

"Avobenzone has been known to be particularly unstable on its own, and a lot of work and reformulation efforts have gone into trying to find ways to stabilize it," said Andrews. "BEMT is significantly more stable."

As with all sunscreens, dermatologists say it's important to reapply every few hours — more frequently if you're swimming or sweating a lot.

Also, people shouldn't rely on sunscreen alone when spending time outside, Stein said. Taking breaks in the shade, wearing a hat and sun-protective clothing are all important protections.

"Sunscreen is just one part of an overall sun-protection plan," Stein said. "Clothing is even better."

articles.title: Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts
articles.summary: New open-source software developed by Microsoft uses machine learning to correct bias in weather forecasts.
articles.body: Old-school physics-based weather forecasting and even new AI models typically become less reliable beyond two weeks, a problem Microsoft claims to have solved using machine learning. Researchers with the company say they’ve found a new, cost-effective way to make more accurate weather forecasts two to six weeks in advance — allowing farmers and emergency responders to plan ahead with greater certainty. The findings were published today in the journal Nature, and the tool is now open-source software. Microsoft joins Google, Nvidia, and other companies developing AI tools for weather forecasting. Instead of creating a new standalone weather model, Microsoft’s latest research in this realm uses machine learning to correct bias in existing models. It’s a more accessible way for resource-strapped weather agencies to improve accuracy using AI, the researchers hope. While physics-based modeling is a resource-intensive endeavor running on supercomputers and generative AI depends on powerful GPUs, Microsoft Research New England senior principal researcher Lester Mackey says the new tool can run just on CPUs. “I have a lot of hope both for the increased resource efficiency of weather forecasting and the extended reliability of forecasts, especially for extreme weather,” Mackey tells The Verge. Physics-based and AI-based models run into similar problems when they start predicting the weather two weeks or more in advance. Traditional models attempt to simulate the complex physics of Earth’s atmosphere, while AI models look for patterns in historical data to make forecasts. In both approaches, models rely on approximations to fill data gaps, whether from regions with sparse weather stations or complex atmospheric phenomena that scientists are still working to understand. The ways in which these models make up for those gaps in data can become a type of systematic bias. The resulting errors compound when making forecasts further ahead in time, making these predictions less precise. Microsoft calls its method Probabilistic Bias Correction (PBC). The tool uses machine learning to identify systematic bias in a model and make corrections. One example Mackey gives is to correct for changes in climate. Greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels are heating up the planet, but a weather model might make predictions based on historical records that can bias it toward colder temperatures than the world is actually experiencing today. The researchers found that PBC improved the accuracy of a leading physics-based weather model by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) for 98 percent of precipitation and 92 percent of temperature targets. The machine learning framework also doubled the accuracy of ECMWF’s new AI forecasting system in the study’s analysis. Before the paper was published, the ECMWF had already awarded the authors’ research on PBC in its AI Weather Quest competition. The new paper on PBC published by researchers at Microsoft, MIT, ECMWF, and other institutions “is a good example of new ideas being developed for the benefit and consideration of the community,” Matthew Chantry, ECMWF’s strategic lead for machine learning, said in an emailed comment to The Verge. “As always, turning ideas into reality [in] an operational process is a most challenging step,” Chantry added. The amount of compute and infrastructure needed for weather forecasting has often left technological advances out of reach for many agencies in economically developing countries. The paper’s authors, however, think PBC can be different. “One of the things that’s really exciting to me about models like PBC is how lightweight they are, how easy to train, that scientists without huge pools of resources can work on trying to configure [these] models and make them perform better in specific localities,” says Genevieve Flaspohler, one of the authors of the paper. Flaspohler worked on PBC as an intern at Microsoft with Mackey, and now she’s the executive director of the nonprofit Rhiza Research, which is working with the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority — with funding from the Gates Foundation — to see whether AI can help get more accurate early warnings out to people. PBC is one of the methods they’re testing ahead of what’s expected to be a more extreme rainy season during a record-breaking El Niño.

articles.title: In 2025, a magnitude-8.8 earthquake ruptured Kamchatka; scientists later used older GPS motion data to map a major locked zone that aligned with the rupture and smaller patches near its starting point
articles.summary: When a magnitude 8.8 earthquake ruptured a fault offshore from Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula in 2025, it sent tsunami waves across the Pacific Ocean.
articles.body: When a magnitude 8.8 earthquake ruptured a fault offshore from Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula in 2025, it sent tsunami waves across the Pacific Ocean. Now researchers have shown that clues to where it would strike may have been sitting in ground-motion measurements collected years earlier. By reanalysing older satellite positioning records, a new study maps a major locked zone on the plate boundary that lines up with the rupture, along with smaller patches near the point where it began. The findings help explain why a comparable earthquake in 1952 unleashed a far more destructive tsunami. Here is what the study found.Where the Pacific Plate slides beneath Kamchatka, the subduction zone behind two great earthquakesKamchatka, a peninsula in the northwest Pacific, marks the place where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. According to the study ‘Linking Interseismic Locking to Coseismic Rupture: The 2025 Mw 8.8 Kamchatka Earthquake’ published in Geophysical Research Letters by Axel Periollat and Gareth Funning, the Pacific Plate descends beneath a smaller piece of crust called the Okhotsk Microplate at roughly 80 millimetres a year, a little over three inches. That sloping contact surface, known as a megathrust, has produced two very large earthquakes in the instrumental era, a magnitude 9.0 event in 1952 and, about 73 years later, the magnitude 8.8 earthquake of 2025. That earthquake was also preceded by smaller foreshocks, a magnitude 7.1 nearly a year earlier and a magnitude 7.4 just days before. The authors describe the 2025 event as a new benchmark against which earlier models of the region's hidden strain can be tested.Locked fault zones explained: How tectonic plates stick together, store strain and release it suddenlyPlates do not glide past each other smoothly everywhere. The study explains that parts of a subduction fault can be locked by friction, so the plates stick while the surrounding rock slowly bends and stores elastic strain, much like a compressed spring. Over the decades to centuries between major earthquakes, which scientists call the interseismic period, that strain accumulates. Other portions of the fault creep, sliding without producing large earthquakes. Mapping which is which matters because locked areas outline where future ruptures could occur. Researchers do this with ground-based satellite positioning receivers, radar measurements from space and estimates of seafloor movement, then build computer models of the fault that reproduce what instruments record at the surface. Comparing those models with what happens during a real earthquake can reveal how a subduction zone is segmented and how it behaves.Older satellite positioning data and how researchers mapped the locked zoneThe team did not start with a map of where they expected trouble. Instead, they used horizontal ground-velocity measurements from satellite positioning stations on the peninsula, compiled in 2005 from receivers that ran continuously for more than four years and from survey stations observed annually between 2001 and 2003. They built a computer model of the fault surface using the Slab2.0 model of the plate interface, then let an algorithm decide which small fault elements were locked. Starting from about 2 percent of elements locked at random, one million independent runs of ten thousand steps each accepted or rejected changes based on how well the model matched the observed motion. Averaging all outcomes produced a probability of locking for every part of the fault.A major locked zone beneath Kamchatka stored enough strain since 1952 to match the energy released in 2025The headline result is a principal locked region made up of 618 fault elements, the largest of six high-probability areas the model identified. In the typical simulation, about 68 per cent of those elements, a median of 423, were locked, and locking probability dropped to low values at depths near 68 kilometres, which fits deeper parts of the fault sliding freely. Assuming plate motion of 80 millimetres a year over roughly 73 years, each locked element would have built up about 5.8 metres of slip deficit, or missing movement. Converted to earthquake size, that stored strain corresponds to magnitudes between 8.85 and 8.99, comparable to the 2025 earthquake's magnitude of 8.84. Scaling by the typical locked fraction still recovers roughly 90 percent of the energy released in 2025, so the zone did not need to be fully locked.Smaller locked patches near the starting point: Why earthquakes may begin at the edges of locked zonesInside the large locked region, the authors used a statistical technique called hierarchical clustering to group fault elements that behaved alike across the million simulations. It split the zone into five sub-areas. The two most strongly locked, with average locking probabilities of about 0.98 and 0.88, lie close to where both the 1952 and 2025 earthquakes began, suggesting these patches may have started ruptures in more than one cycle. Locking only the first three sub-areas reproduced the observed ground motion almost as well as locking the whole region, so a fully locked block is not required. Two large foreshocks, including the magnitude 7.4 event days before the main earthquake, sit near the edges of the locked zone, consistent with rupture often beginning where stress builds fastest.Why the 1952 earthquake caused a far more destructive tsunami than 2025Slip, the distance the two sides of a fault move during an earthquake, tells the tsunami story. The authors compared their locking map with slip models for both events. They found the two earthquakes broke the same deep part of the fault, and the along-strike stretch of high slip looks similar, consistent with repeated failure of one long-lived asperity, a sticky patch on the fault. The difference lies near the trench, the shallow edge of the plate boundary. Tsunami-based models suggest the 1952 earthquake had much larger shallow slip, while the 2025 rupture concentrated deeper with limited shallow slip. The study notes that the 1952 tsunami, with wave heights of 15 to 18 metres in southern Kamchatka and the northern Kuril Islands, was more severe, whereas the 2025 tsunami reached up to about two metres on Hawaiian coasts.Why 2025 slip locally exceeded the strain stored since 1952, and what the 1737 earthquake suggestsThe study also uncovers a puzzle. At 80 millimetres a year, only about 5.8 metres of slip could have accumulated since 1952, yet slip in 2025 locally exceeded 20 to 30 metres. The authors suggest either that part of the strain was never released in 1952, or that other processes, such as slow ground adjustment after the 1952 event, reloaded the fault quickly. Settling it would need analysis of movement after the 2025 earthquake, which lies beyond this paper. Extending the interval to the roughly 215 years between a great 1737 earthquake and 1952 gives a plausible stored deficit equivalent to magnitude 9.1 to 9.3. Smaller earthquakes in between released negligible energy, so most strain is discharged in large megathrust events, the authors conclude.What scientists still need to learn about the fault’s earthquake riskThe authors are candid about limits. Some high-probability patches north of 53 degrees latitude may be artifacts of the analysis, because they vanished when data from a single nearby station were removed, and a deep cluster at about 80 kilometres is likely a modelling edge effect rather than real locking. Earlier models by other researchers agree broadly but differ in the shape and depth of strongly coupled zones, showing how sensitive results are to method. Most importantly, offshore and shallow parts of the fault remain poorly resolved. The authors argue that seafloor geodesy, measuring ground motion on the ocean bottom, is needed to judge rupture and tsunami potential. The work was supported by an award from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
