articles.title: My AI doppelganger tells me what to eat
articles.summary: This week’s Optimizer delves into the concept of digital twins, a virtual version of a patient that can potentially help clinicians model medical treatments.
articles.body: This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here. For the past 100 days or so, my mornings have had a new rhythm. When I wake up, the first thing I have to do is feed my digital twin. It consumes my metabolic data, and its first “meal” of the day is my body composition data, sent straight from a smart scale. Once that’s logged in the app, I scoot over to the kitchen to fill an Owala with lemon water to take my medications with. That, too, gets logged in the app. On Mondays, I’ll follow that up with several calming breaths, measure my blood pressure, and offer that to the digital twin as well. Then it’s time to consider breakfast. I consult my digital twin. My digital twin isn’t so much a robotic clone as it is an AI-powered, color-coded food database that predicts how my glucose levels will react to everything I eat. Red is not so good. Orange is so-so. Green is ideal. It’s built based on the data I feed it, as well as data collected from a continuous glucose monitor. A bowl of protein Cheerios and milk? My digital twin tells me this is orange if eaten alone, but green if I take my daily walk after. So that’s what I decide to eat and do. When that’s all done, I log it in the Twin Health app. In a few hours, the app will generate an insight based on how my glucose reacted, and my “twin” will become more accurate. For now, my twin is fed. Rinse and repeat for roughly another 99 days. Digital twins are a relatively new concept in physical health, both in medicine and sports. It’s a virtual model of a person built from various data points — labs, wearable data, images, genetic profiles, etc. — that is continuously updated over time. Once built, clinicians can then use AI to see how a patient might react to specific medicines or treatments by first “testing” them out on their digital twin. Theoretically, this could also help healthcare providers assess injury risk, predict disease progression, and implement preventive care while minimizing adverse effects for the actual patient. The thought is that this could one day help realize the dream of personalized medicine. Metabolic coaching is perhaps the lowest-stakes, highest-reward version of this technology that can be tested in the real world now. [Image: The white scale is my Twin Health scale. When not building a digital twin, I sometimes use it to help me keep Pablo’s weight in check. My metabolic twin was “born” in June with a giant box from Twin Health delivered to my doorstep. Twin Health is a digital twin program to help people “heal” their metabolisms (e.g., lose weight, manage diabetes, sleep better, etc.). It’s not available for widespread download just yet. Digital twins are still experimental, and currently, this service is only accessible through corporate or private health plans. It’s typically aimed at people with chronic metabolic issues. Twin Health provides everything you need to build a digital twin. Building mine would require 90 days’ worth of Dexcom G7 CGMs, a smart scale, a smart blood pressure cuff, three bottles of multivitamins and magnesium glycinate, and my Apple Watch. That was followed up with a trip to Quest Diagnostics, where a phlebotomist stuck a needle in my arm and sent vials of my blood for further analysis. A few days later, I hopped on Zoom with my Twin Health coach Amanda — a human — and a doctor to review my lab results. Several numbers and formulas were thrown up on a shared screen. As it turns out, my liver? Inflamed, but understandable considering I’ve been diagnosed with a moderate case of nonalcoholic fatty liver. Insulin resistance — definitely there despite ideal HbA1c and fasting glucose tests. My pancreas is apparently working overtime, but my insulin-producing beta cell count seems fine. For now. My triglycerides were also high, though the rest of my lipids looked normal. I knew going in that I inherited a bunk metabolism. A year of testing CGMs as a non-diabetic made that abundantly clear. But after the doctor logged off and Amanda asked me to define my goals, I launched into a spiel about my vague desire to reduce the number of medications I needed to keep my middle-aged metabolism functioning. Could a digital twin help me do that? Maybe. For now, Amanda logged my goal, set up a follow-up call in two weeks, and encouraged me to try logging as many of my meals as possible for the first 30-day period. Once I hit the 90-day mark, I’d be scheduled for another blood draw. [Image: In many ways, I’m relieved my digital twin doesn’t have its own avatar. At least, not one that I can see. I’m glad for the abstract color labels. There’s novelty in going to see what color a cup of pineapple or a turkey hot dog with ketchup and relish might be. (Orange and green, respectively.) At times, I am reminded of Kazuo Ishiguro’s dystopian novel Never Let Me Go, in which clones are raised as organ donors. The scenario isn’t a one-to-one comparison. An AI-powered digital twin can’t actually eat, die, or feel pain. I’m probably anthropomorphizing my discomfort with the idea of “testing” food on a virtual version of my metabolism, as if it were a jester-like food taster in a medieval court. Still, as the months ticked by, I couldn’t help noticing how hungry my digital twin was. And how much that took from me, almost like I was getting drained each time I “fed” my twin. Building this thing takes an immense amount of personal data — even for me, someone who’s used to tracking and reviewing a ton of health data. In my bimonthly check-ins with Amanda, she noted that tracking fatigue was frequent feedback from Twin Health users. My behaviors did change. Both in unexpected and expected ways. Anytime I have to log food, I end up avoiding unhealthy treats more often than not; I don’t feel like getting scolded by apps. That didn’t result in any meaningful weight loss, however. And despite my stated goal of tapering off medications, that ended up not working out quite as smoothly as I’d hoped. I also didn’t learn too many surprises from my digital twin’s metabolic predictions. Though it was validating to see that for me, a bowl of soondubu jjigae and white rice is a solidly green or orange meal, depending on if I’m active after eating. (Take that, low-carb diets. You can pry rice from my cold, dead hands.) I’ve tested far too many CGMs and AI nutrition apps to feel surprised by these insights, though I think it’d be useful for people new to metabolic issues. Twin Health’s bimonthly check-ins did motivate me to get back to training. I’ve always been disciplined in my fitness routines, but the extra accountability of having to state my progress aloud to another human — one who isn’t family — kicked my inner overachiever into gear. After months of feeling too weak from medication side effects, I recently felt strong enough to run an uninterrupted 5K. I’ve also gotten back to strength training with some cajoling from Amanda. [Image: This is an orange food because protein bagels are still bagels. But most importantly, after 100 days, my follow-up labs came back with marked improvements. Amanda says my metabolic health score has jumped by nine points since joining. A year after my doctor’s eyes bugged out at my liver enzymes, all but one are back to normal. These numbers were slowly improving before I tried this whole digital twin business, but they fell faster while trying this whole thing out. My triglycerides dropped by 70mg/dL. There’s been a significant drop in my hs-CRP, which is a biomarker for overall inflammation. I’m still insulin resistant, but less so. I can’t really argue with results like that, can I? I can, actually. The concept of a digital twin is founded on trust. As I said, metabolic use cases are high-reward and low-stakes. If you feed a twin an immense amount of data for losing weight, diabetes management, or more nebulous goals like “better energy” or “better sleep,” failure isn’t immediately life-threatening. There are medications and other avenues to try. Personalized medicine is a different beast. Researchers are looking at digital twins for things beyond metabolism. One area currently being explored, for example, is cancer care and research. There’s massive potential there, particularly when you consider how grueling chemotherapy can be, but also huge challenges. The burden of trust for data privacy, for one. Digital twins are hungry for data, and their accuracy depends on a continuous stream of high-quality and sensitive information about you. That then informs future decision-making. If I felt overwhelmed by three months of logging in a low-stakes environment, how will that translate to higher-stakes scenarios? How does a digital twin exist once treatment is concluded? How does that data “live on” if treatment is unsuccessful? [Image: The CGM experiments continue, as my digital twin hungers for this data. As for me, I’ve decided my digital twin will get to “live” for another three months. Despite my lack of success so far, I haven’t given up on the idea of tapering off some medications. I could also use all the help I can get in getting my liver labs all the way back to normal. Amanda also says I don’t have to be as militant with the data for my twin now that I have a solid foundation. Again, lower stakes mean more flexibility. So, today, I’m asking my digital twin what it thinks about a protein waffle with a tablespoon of peanut butter and some honey, with a side of pineapples. Orange, but again, I can turn it green with a walk.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink terminals
articles.summary: Officials say ability to block Russian drones restricted as Kyiv reels from second night of ballistic missile attacks.
articles.body:
Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite services, disrupting its ability to carry out military operations and leaving Kyiv vulnerable to deadly attacks.

An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that without warning, services had been limited for terminals travelling over 100mph overnight on Wednesday – effectively limiting Ukraine’s ability to launch drones, which use satellite internet to pilot the craft.

Writing on Telegram, defence technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Ukraine was “deprived of one of the few chances to defend itself from Shahed drones”.

He added that frontline logistics and long-distance missions were also disrupted.

The suggestion that Elon Musk’s company had throttled Starlink services drew the ire of Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv’s behalf.

“Hey Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” wrote Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister. “As your European customers, we are watching you.”

The “big man” jibe refers to a public dispute on social media between Musk, Sikorski and United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio in 2025, when the SpaceX boss told Sikorski to “ be quiet, small man ” on his X platform.

The clash broke out when Musk, the trillionaire former senior adviser to US President Donald Trump and key midterm election donor for his Republican Party, said that Ukraine’s “entire frontline could collapse” if he switched off Starlink.

He later said, “No matter how much I disagree with the Ukraine policy, Starlink will never turn off its terminals … We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.”

The slowdown comes after Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv for the second night in a row, killing at least nine people and damaging electricity and heating infrastructure.

Zelenskyy says Ukraine did not receive its usual warnings from Western allies, without specifying which partners.

Trump said the US has not stopped sharing intelligence.

Beskrestnov warned that the slowdown “cannot be a coincidence” after Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel – despite international sanctions to isolate Moscow.

Speaking to AFP, another Ukrainian official accused Washington of throttling Starlink and helping Russia.

On Saturday, Trump suggested Zelenskyy had not done enough to end the war with Russia, blaming him for high diesel prices in the US.

articles.title: Dozens of California dams need repair as El Niño winter draws closer
articles.summary: With an El Niño winter threatening heavy rain, the State Auditor warns that California’s aging dams “continue to pose a risk to public safety,” especially in the Bay Area, San Diego, and Los Angeles areas.
articles.body: With an El Niño winter threatening heavy rain, the State Auditor warns that California’s aging dams “continue to pose a risk to public safety,” especially in the Bay Area, San Diego, and Los Angeles areas. Lawmakers gave the state the power to penalize dam owners that violate safety requirements in 2017, after the Oroville spillway failure forced the evacuation of nearly 200,000 people. Water managers have yet to use that power, the audit found. Even if state water managers had wielded their enforcement powers, dam owners likely couldn’t have afforded the fixes. An audit released Monday found 57 dams in poor or unsatisfactory condition as of May, up from previous counts. That number is likely to keep rising, as state water officials reevaluate aging dams. The 40 riskiest dams — rated high or extremely high hazard — are located throughout the state, but cluster near densely populated coastal cities. Should these dams fail, the auditor reported, “they could collectively endanger as many as 1.5 million people and cause more than $265 billion in economic damage.” Almost a decade ago, lawmakers strengthened the California Department of Water Resources’ authority to impose penalties such as reservoir restrictions, property liens, and fines when dam owners violate state safety laws and other requirements. State engineers have referred owners of 44 dams for enforcement as of April. But, the auditor wrote, the water resources department “has never taken punitive enforcement actions against dam owners that fail to remedy their violations.” Aging dams, limited funds The problem is that dams are getting older. Many were built when safety standards were softer. State laws never required dam owners to set aside funds to keep them safe, so when concrete crumbles, sediment accumulates and spillways threaten to erode under floodwaters, most dam owners lack the money for repairs. The state’s water resources department oversees the safety of more than 1,220 dams, most of them in satisfactory condition. Responsibility for maintaining the dams falls to the local governments, utilities, water agencies, and the private landowners and companies that own them. Some of the dams rated in poor condition are owned by state agencies. Disasters are extremely rare. But when they do occur, like in Oroville, or the 1928 collapse of nearly-new St. Francis dam northwest of Los Angeles — they can be catastrophic. The auditor applauded the water resources department’s inspection program but blasted its failure to enforce against dam owners who fail to meet state planning, safety or other requirements, “thereby allowing serious deficiencies to persist.” One of the cases involved a dam with a 47-foot-wide hole in its spillway that has gone unrepaired for more than 30 years, which the audit said could cause flooding affecting nearly 300 people and more than $88 million in damage. The audit doesn’t name the dam. State water managers said more specifics could pose security concerns, though the department makes each dam’s hazard potential and condition public in an annual report. State water managers finalized the enforcement regulations in 2022. But they told the auditor they haven’t been able to adequately staff an enforcement branch and aren’t confident they could afford to defend their actions in a hearing. Even with staff and money, the auditor concludes, if a dam owner remained noncompliant, the state “cannot act before the dam poses emergency-level danger. This leaves a gap in state law that puts public safety at risk.” Drop in the bucket Gov. Gavin Newsom touted dam repairs in his drought-era water supply strategy four years ago, as a way to shore up water supplies. Two years later, in 2024, Newsom and lawmakers slashed funding for a dam repair grant program. Since then, a 2024 ballot proposition delivered a $464 million infusion for the program. A Federal Emergency Management Agency grant also awarded California $629,198 this September, according to Jason Ince, a spokesperson for the Department of Water Resources. But the audit cited estimates that repairing the state’s less-than-satisfactory dams could cost around $28 billion, making the funding a drop in the bucket. The report urged state lawmakers to set deadlines and require dam owners with high and extremely high hazard dams — meaning ones that could kill people if they fail — to submit maintenance and repair plans to state agencies. It also called for lawmakers to expand state water managers’ enforcement authority, and for the agency to use the full force of its powers. “To ensure that the safety of the public is addressed before a dam’s condition results in an emergency,” the audit said, “the Legislature should amend state law to allow Water Resources to order the condemnation and decommissioning of a dam when Water Resources’ other means of enforcement are unsuccessful.” Laura Hollender, deputy director of flood management and safety with the Department of Water Resources, said that the department worked closely with the State Auditor but disagrees with some of the report’s findings and recommendations. Still, she said in a statement, they are carefully reviewing the recommendations and preparing for whatever El Niño brings. “Protecting public safety is DWR’s highest priority, and we recognize the critical role that dam safety and levee maintenance play in reducing flood risk for California communities.” As the wet season approaches, the auditor also highlighted that dam safety planning statewide is incomplete. The Governor’s Office of Emergency Service has not yet approved emergency plans for 245 dams describing what their owners would do to protect people and property should the dam fail. Officials told the auditor’s office that dam owners haven’t completed required revisions, and state law doesn’t require deadlines. ___ This story was originally published by CalMatters and distributed through a partnership with The Associated Press.

articles.title: Ambrosia Energy will build a 10 GWh factory in Texas to make batteries for off-grid data centers | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Startup Ambrosia Energy will build a massive factory to crank out batteries to augment solar panels, creating a round-the-clock clean power plant.
articles.body:
Ambrosia Energy has begun work on a massive, 10 gigawatt-hour battery factory near Austin, Texas, co-founder and CEO Ben Longmier announced onstage Tuesday at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco.

“That allows us to build about a 300 megawatt power plant per year out at our field sites,” he said.

The factory will occupy 150,000 square feet, and Longmier said that Ambrosia plans to reach full production in two to three years.

The startup emerged from stealth in June to build power plants for data centers at a cost of $100 per megawatt hour. Longmier and his co-founder, Sara Spangelo, had settled on solar plus batteries as the cheapest option that’s the fastest to deploy. Solar panels power the load during the day and charge the batteries, which discharge at night and on cloudy days to keep the data center operating round the clock.

Longmier and Spangelo previously founded the satellite constellation startup Swarm, which they sold to SpaceX.

Ambrosia is also beginning work on its first commercial power plant in West Texas later this year, Longmier said. The facility will pair 300 megawatts of solar panels with 660 megawatt-hours of batteries to deliver 30 megawatts of continuous power, with a goal of 99.3% uptime.

Even with “overbuilding” solar and batteries to deliver continuous uptime, Longmier said the company can be profitable at $100 per megawatt-hour, making it competitive with natural gas turbines that many hyperscalers are planning to use to power their data centers.

Sections of Ambrosia’s first pilot-scale power plant have been operating continuously for more than 100 days, Longmier said. The pilot is capable of generating 200 kilowatts of electricity 24/7.

To hit its cost targets, Ambrosia has been finding ways to simplify its components, including solar mounts and battery packs. By reducing part counts, and manufacturing many components in a factory, the startup has been able to reduce costs relative to buying from outside suppliers.

“We buy existing cells and we make our own pack in-house, and it has the fewest parts by a factor of about 100 compared to any other competitor we’ve seen,” Longmier said. ”We’ve been able to get to about 1.3x the cost of the bare cell compared to about a 5- or 7x for most stationary storage systems.”

articles.title: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?
articles.summary: It is the "backbone of military communications in Ukraine" that provides vital high-speed internet to forces across the country.
articles.body:
Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.

Kyiv has adopted it as a vital battlefield communications tool and also uses it in drone warfare.

Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones are able to maintain stronger connections with operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.

But a sudden speed restriction for drones connected to Starlink means some battlefield "missions" have been disrupted, according to a top Ukrainian official.

Serhiy Beskrestnov also said officials had not been told about the 100mph (160km/h) speed limits set overnight on Tuesday by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.

Throttling drones connected to the network at this relatively low speed makes Ukrainian efforts to intercept jet-powered Russian drones all but useless, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).

Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.

Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized."

Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network.

Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said.

Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.

Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need.

The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine.

Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.

President Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk.

Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX.

Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.

And in a post on X , Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology.

"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.

"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train , but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders .

articles.title: Russia’s frozen hinterlands have long been feared to harbor disease risks
articles.summary: The unexplained death this month of a Russian lab technician at a Siberian facility for the study of dangerous pathogens raised global anxieties over the pot...
articles.body:
Russia’s frozen hinterlands have long been feared to harbor disease risks

The unexplained death this month of a Russian lab technician at a Siberian facility for the study of dangerous pathogens raised global anxieties over the potential for an outbreak of pneumonic plague.

But while the cause of concern - bound up in a lack of transparency from Moscow - was new, Russia's frozen hinterlands have long been the source of a separate fear that they could harbor disease risks for which the world is not prepared.

Russian authorities imposed containment measures after the 28-year-old's death from what they said was pneumonia of "unknown origins," prompting the United States to ask for more information. A World Health Organization report released Saturday said that Russian authorities found no signs of an outbreak of plague or some other infectious disease, but did not provide sufficient details to identify the origin of the woman's illness or say whether exposure at work played a role in it.

Siberia's vast wilderness harbors natural reservoirs of pathogens, from fleas that spread plague found in marmots and squirrels to ticks bearing encephalitis to the ancient pathogens frozen in the layer of permafrost.

The Russian institute where the lab technician worked was set up in the 1930s as a plague prevention station to curb outbreaks of the deadly bacterial disease that periodically affected local populations as well as people in neighboring Mongolia and China's Manchuria region. The disease, for which early antibiotic treatments were pioneered that decade, could be spread through contact with marmots, which were hunted for meat and sometimes eaten undercooked or even raw, like in a 2019 case of a Mongolian couple.

The settlement of Siberia, which had a 19th-century gold rush and served as a place of exile for criminals under the Russian Empire, connected the remote region to the western parts of the empire and raised the risk of plague spreading farther west, much as epidemic diseases from European Russia, such as cholera and typhus, easily reached Siberia through migrating workers and because of the near-total absence of medical care.

A study published this year suggested that the bands of hunter-gatherers who inhabited the Lake Baikal region were the victims of the earliest known plague outbreak, about 5,500 years ago. To this day, plague remains endemic in parts of Siberia and the Russian Far East, where the bacterium persists naturally among wild rodents.

Human cases in Russia are rare, however. The country's last recorded human infection was in 2016, when a 10-year-old boy in the Altai region contracted plague after contact with a marmot.

The threat of dangerous disease comes not only from wildlife but also from the millennia-old microbes and viruses stored in the permafrost that underlies the vast majority of the region.

About a decade ago, a group of researchers isolated "zombie viruses" from Siberian permafrost, raising fears that a new global medical emergency could be triggered by a disease from the distant past.

The permafrost, a dark, cold, oxygenless mass, is a perfect storage container for biological material, and scientists believe that at its deepest levels it may contain viruses up to a million years old, far older than Homo sapiens , the modern human species.

In 2023, the researchers - led by Jean-Michel Claverie of Aix-Marseille University in France - published a landmark study in the journal Viruses documenting the revival of ancient viruses from the Siberian permafrost.

The report warned that accelerating permafrost thaw caused by climate change poses a potential public health threat by releasing dormant pathogens. Claverie's team isolated 13 ancient viruses taken from locations across Siberia, belonging to five new viral groups. The oldest, a Pandoravirus yedoma , had been frozen solid beneath an underground lake for 48,500 years, while other, younger strains (around 27,000 years old) were extracted from the remains of a woolly mammoth's stomach and from mammoth wool.

Other researchers have noted that although the revived viruses were able to infect amoebas in lab conditions, it is unclear whether such viruses could infect animals or humans, or find a host outside a controlled laboratory.

Claverie and his team cautioned at the time that unknowns remain buried in the permafrost, and a warming climate, which would also open previously untouched lands to deeper development, could expose people to pathogens that affect humans.

In 2016, climate change played a role in unleashing anthrax in the remote Yamalo-Nenets region of Siberia, experts said at the time. Unusually high temperatures that summer, soaring to 95 degrees Fahrenheit, melted permafrost, and according to one hypothesis, exposed an infected reindeer carcass. The pathogen spread to living reindeer and eventually to a community of nomadic herders, where a 12-year-old boy died.

articles.title: In 1930, a Pittsburgh plumber built a tiny aluminium observatory in his backyard for a homemade telescope; its unusual dome became a prototype for observatory designs and later helped bring him face to face with Einstein
articles.summary: In the autumn of 1930, Leo Scanlon, a plumber from Pittsburgh, solved a problem in his backyard that would leave a lasting mark on amateur astronomy.
articles.body: In the autumn of 1930, Leo Scanlon, a plumber from Pittsburgh, solved a problem in his backyard that would leave a lasting mark on amateur astronomy. Scanlon was building a private observatory behind his home in the Summer Hill neighbourhood on Pittsburgh's North Side. He needed a lightweight, weather-resistant dome to protect a homemade telescope. Instead of using heavy wood or steel, he tried a material rarely used in construction at the time: sheet aluminium. The result was the Valley View Observatory, which featured what was described as the world's first all-aluminium observatory dome. Its design became a model for later astronomy facilities and helped Scanlon secure a personal meeting with Albert Einstein four years later.Solving a weight problem behind a terrace houseAccording to historical records kept in the Stellafane convention archives, Scanlon began recording daily notes about his backyard project in September 1930. Working with a friend named Bud, he drew plans for a rotating dome that did not need an internal support frame. Instead of using heavy iron supports, Scanlon joined curved sheets of aluminium with specially folded seams on the outside. This made the dome much lighter than traditional wooden structures. It could turn smoothly on rollers placed on top of a simple, eight-sided wooden building. To test the strength of the finished dome, Scanlon sat on top of it after fitting the final metal panels. Site records show that the entire observatory cost $250 to build, with $178 spent on the aluminium dome itself. The Valley View Observatory officially opened on 4 October 1930. Its rotating dome protected Scanlon's reflecting telescope and allowed him to observe the night sky over Pittsburgh.Founding a regional astronomy movementThe completed aluminium dome helped Scanlon move from being a keen hobbyist to becoming a recognised figure in the amateur astronomy community across the United States. In 1929, Scanlon co-founded the Amateur Astronomers' Association of Pittsburgh (AAAP). The group aimed to support people who studied astronomy on their own and those who built their own telescopes. Historical records published by the AAAP note that Scanlon's backyard observatory soon became a meeting place for amateur astronomers, people who worked with optical equipment and professional astronomers visiting western Pennsylvania. His aluminium dome design attracted interest from telescope makers across the country. They valued its light weight, resistance to rust and corrosion, low maintenance needs and ease of rotation. These features helped make aluminium a common choice for domes at smaller observatories.Meeting Albert Einstein in PittsburghScanlon's standing among local amateur scientists helped lead to a meeting with Albert Einstein in December 1934. Einstein travelled to Pittsburgh to give a major lecture on his theory of relativity at the Carnegie Institute of Technology, now Carnegie Mellon University. According to historical accounts published by Carnegie Mellon University News, local organisers arranged a busy schedule for the famous physicist. However, Einstein also asked for time to meet amateur researchers and working people with an interest in science. As a co-founder of the Amateur Astronomers' Association of Pittsburgh, Scanlon was invited to meet Einstein during his visit. He personally invited the Nobel Prize winner to see the group's astronomy exhibits and instruments. Historical commentary preserved in Carnegie Mellon's archives notes that Einstein respected amateur scientists who pursued research because of their genuine interest in the subject. He reportedly appreciated meeting ordinary people who spent their free time studying the universe.Legacy of an astronomical pioneerThe original Valley View Observatory remained in Pittsburgh for nearly seven decades. It was dismantled in August 1997, but preservationists and members of the Amateur Astronomers' Association of Pittsburgh saved the historic aluminium dome to protect it for the future. Scanlon's contribution to amateur science and astronomy education also received recognition from the international scientific community. Main-belt asteroid 8131, discovered by astronomers in 1976, was later officially named "Scanlon" in his honour. Through a backyard building project and his work bringing astronomy enthusiasts together, the Pittsburgh plumber showed how practical skills and a passion for science could make a lasting contribution to astronomical research and facilities.

articles.title: In 2021, 1,000 Swiss volunteers buried 2,000 pairs of underwear; Ontario farmer tested soil health on his 500-acre farm from 2015 to 2025; study finds cotton decomposes fastest in gardens, slowest on lawns
articles.summary: A pair of cotton underwear may seem an unlikely tool for measuring soil health, but scientists and farmers are using the unusual experiment to understand
articles.body: A pair of cotton underwear may seem an unlikely tool for measuring soil health, but scientists and farmers are using the unusual experiment to understand what lies beneath the ground. From a Canadian farmer who discovered changes in his soil over a decade to a Swiss research project involving more than 1,000 volunteers, the “Soil Your Undies” initiative is drawing attention to the importance of healthy, biologically active soil.Norm Lamothe and his family operate a 500-acre farm outside Peterborough, Ontario, in Canada. In 2015, Lamothe learned about the “Soil Your Undies” campaign launched by the Soil Conservation Council of Canada and decided to try the experiment himself.The idea was simple: bury a pair of cotton underpants in the soil, leave them underground for a few months and then dig them up to see how much they had decomposed.Agricultural experts explained that the breakdown of the cotton could offer a rough indication of microbial activity. Healthy soil contains microorganisms that feed on organic matter, including cotton fibres. The more the underwear decomposes, the greater the evidence of biological activity in the soil.However, Lamothe was disappointed by what he found when he first retrieved his underwear. His white Hanes underpants were still largely intact.“That’s really what started my journey down the soil health path,” Lamothe told The Narwhal. “Much to our chagrin, they were completely intact.”The result prompted him to look more closely at the condition of his farm’s soil and explore practices that could improve its biological health.Crop rotation and sheep help improve soil conditionsFollowing the initial experiment, Lamothe joined farmer peer groups, including the Ontario Soil Network and Farmers for Climate Solutions, to learn more about soil conservation.He began diversifying his crop rotation, growing corn, soybeans, winter wheat and oats. This was twice the variety he had previously cultivated, helping reduce reliance on a narrower selection of crops.He also introduced hay to help prevent erosion and keep the soil anchored. In 2022, he brought sheep onto the farm to graze the hay. Their manure helped return nutrients to the ground.These changes were part of a broader effort to improve the soil’s condition through more diverse agricultural practices and natural nutrient cycling.A decade after his first attempt, Lamothe repeated the underwear experiment. This time, the results were different: the cotton had decomposed considerably more.“Whether the change came from our practices or differing weather conditions is up for debate, but certainly we saw we had microbial activity,” Lamothe told The Narwhal.The retrieved underwear now hangs framed in his office, serving as an unusual conversation starter for visitors curious about why a farmer would display a pair of old underpants.Why scientists say healthy soil needs billions of microbesThe idea behind the experiment is rooted in the role microorganisms play in maintaining healthy soil. Bacteria, fungi and other soil organisms break down organic matter, recycle nutrients and support the processes that help plants grow.The United States Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service has also promoted the experiment, providing guidance for farmers and gardeners interested in examining soil health.“Healthy soil contains billions of microbes that consume the cotton,” the agency explains in its guidance. It also notes that one teaspoon of healthy soil contains more microbes than there are people on the planet.Beyond decomposing organic matter, these organisms help soil resist erosion, cycle nutrients and store water. These functions are important for agriculture and for the wider environment.The underwear test is not a complete scientific assessment of soil quality, however. Decomposition can also be influenced by weather, soil moisture, temperature, the type of soil and the length of time the cotton remains buried. It is best understood as a simple indicator of biological activity rather than a definitive measure of overall soil health.Swiss researchers bury more than 2,000 pairs of underwearThe experiment has also become a citizen science project. In 2021, researchers from Agroscope, Switzerland’s federal centre of excellence for agricultural research, collaborated with scientists from the University of Zurich on a project called “Proof by Underpants”.The initiative recruited more than 1,000 volunteers across Switzerland to bury cotton underwear and tea bags at locations throughout the country.Participants buried more than 2,000 pairs of underpants and 12,000 tea bags at nearly 1,000 sites. After two months, they dug up the materials and sent the underwear, along with accompanying soil samples, to the University of Zurich laboratory for analysis.The large-scale experiment allowed researchers to compare decomposition across different environments, offering insight into how soil management and land use affect biological activity.Gardens have the fastest soil decomposition ratesThe study’s findings, published on August 26, revealed differences in decomposition rates across land types. Private gardens showed the fastest decomposition, while lawns recorded the slowest. Agricultural fields and meadows fell between the two.The results highlighted how the condition and management of soil can influence the organisms responsible for breaking down organic matter.“Our results show that how soil is managed can significantly affect both soil life and soil quality,” said study co-leader Marcel van der Heijden, a professor of agroecology at the University of Zurich.“Healthy, biologically active soil is crucial for fertility, nutrient cycling, and many other ecosystem services,” he added.The project also benefited participants, who received individual feedback based on their samples to help them make more sustainable decisions about managing their gardens and other land.‘Underpants Index’ could make soil science more accessibleThe Swiss researchers said the experiment demonstrated how an ordinary cotton garment could help make a complex scientific subject easier for the public to understand.“Overall, this project demonstrates that underpants can serve as a simple and easy-to-interpret tool, providing informative insights into the state of soils,” the researchers wrote in their study, published in the scientific journal Plants, People, Planet.They proposed an “Underpants Index” as an accessible way to assess soil decomposition processes, offer clues about soil fertility and raise awareness about soil as a vital but threatened resource.Although burying underwear cannot replace laboratory testing or a comprehensive soil assessment, the experiment offers farmers, gardeners and researchers an engaging way to observe biological activity.

articles.body:
Confusion swirls around Starlink restrictions in Ukraine

Elon Musk’s Starlink became embroiled in controversy Wednesday after Ukraine’s military faced restricted access to the satellite-based system .

A source familiar with the matter told The Hill that Starlink services were cut off for objects that traveled more than 100 miles an hour, impacting the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters .

This sparked a barrage of questions and concerns online, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) calling on Musk in a social media post to explain the incident.

The SpaceX and Tesla CEO said Wednesday that decisions to restrict the speed or usage of Starshield , Starlink’s military system, are made by the U.S. military and, ultimately, the president.

It is not clear at this point what caused Ukraine’s military to lose access to the system, which is owned and controlled by the U.S. government.

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote in a comment on the social platform X, which he owns.

“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company,” Musk said.

By Wednesday afternoon, Ukraine’s defense minister said SpaceX was working to restore satellite speeds.

articles.title: Ukraine claims SpaceX is throttling Starlink again amid war with Russia. Musk says ask POTUS.
articles.summary: Elon Musk-owned SpaceX is reportedly restricting speed for Starlink satellite internet terminals used by Ukraine amid Russia's ongoing invasion of the countr...
articles.body:
Early on Wednesday, Ukraine claimed that SpaceX ( SPCX ) was restricting speed for Starlink satellite internet terminals used by Ukraine amid Russia's ongoing invasion of the country, the Wall Street Journal reported .

"I confirm that SpaceX implemented a speed limit for Starlink terminals operating in motion last night," said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, according to WSJ. "Our defense forces received no warning about this restriction, and it has led to the disruption of a number of missions."

Starlink, essentially a global broadband internet service delivered from space, is a core part of SpaceX's business . There are more than 10 million Starlink subscribers worldwide, and SpaceX is now moving to challenge legacy wireless carriers.

Ukrainian military drone crews and logistics operations regularly leverage Starlink to provide video feeds and precise targeting. WSJ reported that "Ukraine's access to SpaceX's StarShield — a Starlink subscription designed for government and military use — is provided under a contract handled by the Defense Department."

On Wednesday afternoon, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk stated that SpaceX was not involved in the latest decision to restrict those specific services.

A senior US official then told Barik Ravid of Axios that the Trump administration had nothing to do with any Starlink service constraints.

In any case, this is not the first time Ukraine has experienced Starlink throttling, though it is the first since SpaceX became a public company this summer.

In 2022, as Ukraine retook territory from Russia, Musk reportedly ordered SpaceX engineers to cut some Starlink coverage in contested areas of Ukraine. In 2023, the company acknowledged efforts to throttle Starlink usage during the war.

"There are things that we can do to limit their ability to [leverage Starlink]," Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and COO, said at the time. "There are things that we can do, and have done."

Musk is an ally of President Trump, who has recently ramped up criticism of Zelensky. Ukraine also bombed Russian data centers recently, disrupting bot traffic on Musk-owned X and other social media platforms.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who is not running for reelection and supports the US backing Ukraine's defense, posted on X — which Musk owns — seeking clarification on SpaceX's policy related to Starlink services.

articles.title: A detector buried nearly a mile underground records an unexplained particle interaction in the hunt for dark matter
articles.summary: Scientists working on the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) dark matter experiment have identified a single particle interaction that they have struggled to explain using
articles.body: Scientists working on the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) dark matter experiment have identified a single particle interaction that they have struggled to explain using any known background process. The detector operates nearly a mile underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, US, where it searches for signs of dark matter.The result is the most compelling hint of dark matter reported by the experiment so far, although it does not meet the statistical threshold required to claim a discovery. Dark matter is thought to make up around 85% of all matter in the universe, yet it has never been directly detected.According to UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), the analysis was led by the University of Bristol and presented at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics conference in Japan.What did the underground detector discover in its search for dark matterThe LZ experiment identified a single particle interaction in a region of its dataset that researchers had not previously explored. The team spent months investigating possible causes, including known background processes that can produce signals inside the detector.The event stands out because researchers understand the detector and its background signals well, making an unexplained interaction important to investigate.However, the finding does not confirm the presence of dark matter. The result has a statistical significance of 2.6 sigma, indicating a roughly 0.5% chance that known background processes alone could explain the event. Physics requires a significance of 5 sigma before a result can be declared a discovery.How the LZ detector searches for dark matter deep undergroundThe LZ experiment uses 10 tonnes of ultrapure liquid xenon to search for weakly interacting massive particles, known as WIMPs. These hypothetical particles are among the candidates researchers investigate in the search for dark matter. The detector operates nearly a mile underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, US.The experiment is managed by the US Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and brings together around 250 scientists and engineers from 39 institutions worldwide. Researchers look for rare interactions that might provide evidence of dark matter.What could the unexplained particle interaction tell scientists about dark matterIf the event was the result of a dark matter interaction, it would point to a WIMP with a mass of at least 200 GeV/c² (gigaelectron volts), making it more than 200 times the mass of a proton. Its interaction with ordinary matter would fall outside the simplest theoretical models.However, researchers have not confirmed that the signal came from dark matter. Rick Gaitskell, a professor at Brown University and the LZ spokesperson, said, “We’re very intrigued to see this event in the data, in the region where we expect dark matter to show up and the competing backgrounds are very low”.“With only one event, we don’t want to get ahead of ourselves. We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input”.How the LZ team plans to investigate the signal and advance dark matter researchThe LZ collaboration will continue collecting data at the Sanford Underground Research Facility to determine whether the signal grows stronger, weakens or disappears as more observations become available. The UK has played a central role in the experiment, with 10 teams contributing to its construction and operations and around 50 UK researchers involved in operations, data analysis and collaboration leadership since commissioning in 2021.The UK team is also working with international partners on XENON-LUX-ZEPLIN-DARWIN, a next-generation rare-event observatory designed for dark matter detection and neutrino physics. The project currently receives support through a UKRI Infrastructure Fund preliminary activity. The UK is also exploring the possibility of hosting the experiment at the Boulby Underground Laboratory, supporting plans for further research into rare particle interactions.

articles.title: U.S. may have withheld warnings to Ukraine on deadly Kyiv strikes
articles.summary: The Trump administration may have withheld intelligence warnings to Ukraine about Russian strikes that killed 6 and cut power to 600,000 people, sources say.
articles.body:
The U.S. may have intentionally withheld early warnings this week of Russian strikes on Ukraine , multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning from our partners" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage at Kyiv and other locations early Tuesday.

The sources said American officials told their Ukrainian counterparts the system used to detect Russian missile launches had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the topic, told CBS News they did not believe the excuse, and they accused the U.S. instead of "playing" with the system.

When Russia launched another wave of ballistic missiles around 3 a.m. local time on Wednesday, the sources said the U.S. early warning system appeared to be working again.

The sources said the U.S. had failed to provide intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches during one previous instance earlier this year, citing the need to focus more resources on the Middle East.

Zelenskyy said Wednesday that Russia launched more than 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions during the overnight attack, primarily targeting energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power.

President Trump, asked Tuesday if the U.S. had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, said: "No, we haven't. We help them, but we're really helping them get to a final answer. We want the war ended."

"We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end," Mr. Trump said.

Russia started launching strikes soon after Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire."

Earlier this week, the Trump administration threatened to stop sharing intelligence and to halt the purchase of U.S.-made weapons by European allies for Ukraine via the PURL procurement system if Ukraine did not stop deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, a European and a Ukrainian official told CBS News.

Ukraine relies on U.S. intelligence for both offensive and defensive military capabilities, including data from satellites and aircraft sensors used to identify launches of Russian aircraft and missiles. Sources familiar with the matter told CBS News the U.S. had not ceased intelligence sharing with Ukraine overall — calling the lack of a warning about this week's attacks a specific incident.

Ukrainian officials and soldiers also told CBS News that Ukraine's military had started experiencing difficulties Tuesday night and Wednesday morning with Starlink, the satellite technology owned by SpaceX's Elon Musk.

In an interview with CBS News earlier this year, Ukraine's former minister of defense Mykhailo Fedorov said Starlink was one of Ukraine's most important technologies, as it allows Ukrainian soldiers to communicate and carry out strikes in environments saturated by electronic warfare.

"On the night of 14 October, without warning the Defence Forces, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals ('military package') while in motion. This complicates UAV missions, particularly interceptors and middle-strike drones, and reduces capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance and signal relay," sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense told CBS News. "At present, the Ministry of Defence is in contact with the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners, is collecting data from all units, and backup communication channels are being tested and put into use."

The Starlink restrictions were first reported by the Kyiv Independent and the Financial Times. CBS News has reached out to SpaceX, the White House, and the Pentagon for comment.

On Wednesday, as President Zelenskyy arrived in the United Kingdom to meet with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other officials, he called for a U.S. response to the recent Russian strikes.

"The strike was absolutely deliberate and indicative in its scale — such a demonstrative disrespect from Russia toward America has never happened before. Russia does not consider the statements of the President of America to be strong," he wrote on X. "We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not close their eyes to reality to respond, and to respond harshly."

articles.title: Ponte desaba e deixa moradores ilhados em condomínio de luxo em MS | G1
articles.standfirst: Acesso ao Nasa Park I foi levado pela enxurrada após as chuvas; prefeitura mobilizou equipes para avaliar os danos e restabelecer a passagem.
articles.summary: Acesso ao Nasa Park I foi levado pela enxurrada após as chuvas; prefeitura mobilizou equipes para avaliar os danos e restabelecer a passagem.
articles.body:
Moradores do condomínio de luxo Nasa Park I, localizado entre Campo Grande e Jaraguari , estão ilhados após as chuvas registradas entre quarta-feira (14) e quinta-feira (15). A ponte que dá acesso ao residencial foi levada pela enxurrada e, sem outra via de acesso, os moradores não conseguem deixar o local.

Esta é a segunda vez que os moradores enfrentam uma situação de isolamento. Em agosto de 2024, o rompimento de uma represa na região destruiu uma passagem de acesso ao condomínio. Na ocasião, a água invadiu casas e atingiu parte da BR-163. A represa tinha mais de 20 hectares de lâmina d'água e ficava entre aproximadamente 100 casas de luxo.

Em nota, a Prefeitura de Jaraguari informou que tomou conhecimento dos danos na manhã desta quinta-feira e adotou providências para avaliar a situação e restabelecer o acesso. Entre as medidas estão a realização de uma avaliação técnica para identificar os danos e os riscos, além da mobilização de equipes e maquinários para executar os serviços necessários, assim que as condições climáticas permitirem.

Segundo o prefeito Cláudio Ferreira da Silva, equipes de infraestrutura, engenharia e Defesa Civil estão no local para realizar os levantamentos necessários. Ele explicou que apenas o Nasa Park I está com o acesso impedido. O condomínio Nasa Park II não foi afetado, pois conta com duas vias secundárias de acesso e está localizado antes do trecho onde a ponte caiu.

Moradores relatam dificuldades para deixar o condomínio

Uma moradora do residencial, Karolaine de Novaes, disse ao g1 que a ponte caiu durante a madrugada. Ela percebeu a situação ao sair de casa pela manhã. Karolaine precisava levar a filha, de dois meses, para tomar uma vacina, mas não conseguiu deixar o condomínio. Segundo ela, não há outra saída disponível para os moradores.

Outro morador, que preferiu não se identificar, afirmou que as condições tornam inviável a saída do local. Ele relatou que um caseiro de uma propriedade vizinha tentou atravessar o trecho a pé, mas precisou retornar porque a água chegava à cintura.

Segundo o morador, a única passagem disponível, que desabou nesta quinta-feira, ficava dentro de uma propriedade privada e havia sido cedida para o uso dos residentes.

Outra reclamação do morador diz respeito à presença de animais em áreas de convivência do condomínio. Segundo ele, desde o rompimento da represa, animais de propriedades rurais vizinhas e da fauna local passaram a entrar nesses espaços, o que, conforme o relato, representa riscos à saúde dos moradores devido à proximidade com os animais.

articles.title: Microplastics found in 95% of sampled sea snakes along UAE’s Sharjah coast; study examined 6 species and identified 390 particles
articles.summary: Microplastics have been detected in nearly all the stranded sea snakes examined in a study covering the Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman coasts of Sharjah,
articles.body: Microplastics have been detected in nearly all the stranded sea snakes examined in a study covering the Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman coasts of Sharjah, United Arab Emirates. In Microplastic ingestion in sea snakes: Examining age-related exposure and regional differences, published online on 21 November 2025 in the Journal of Hazardous Materials: Plastics, researchers examined the gastrointestinal tracts of 63 dead, stranded snakes belonging to 6 species. They detected microplastics in 60 of the 63 specimens, and fibres accounted for 96.9% of the 390 particles identified. The authors describe the research as the first published study of microplastic ingestion in sea snakes. Although the findings establish that the sampled animals had ingested microplastics, they do not establish whether the particles harmed the snakes or identify the precise source of the contamination. Future studies tracing the particles to their sources and testing for biological effects could reveal whether microplastic ingestion actually threatens sea snake health, and whether limiting laundry wastewater pollution might reduce exposure along the Gulf coasts.Microplastics in sea snakes: how researchers examined 63 stranded animalsThe research team examined 63 sea snakes collected between the beginning of 2018 and the end of 2021 through Sharjah’s strandings-response programme. All the specimens included in the analysis were already dead when collected. The researchers examined their gastrointestinal tracts to identify and measure ingested microplastics. The sample comprised 6 species, although the numbers varied considerably between them. The Arabian Gulf coral reef sea snake (Hydrophis lapemoides) accounted for 39 specimens, while the yellow-bellied sea snake (Hydrophis platurus) accounted for 14. The remaining animals comprised 4 yellow sea snakes (Hydrophis spiralis), 3 ornate sea snakes (Hydrophis ornatus), 2 annulated sea snakes (Hydrophis cyanocinctus) and 1 spine-bellied sea snake (Hydrophis curtus).The specimens came from Sharjah’s coasts along the Arabian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. The sample included 39 snakes from the Arabian Gulf and 24 from the Gulf of Oman. The findings therefore describe the sampled animals from Sharjah, not sea snakes across either entire region.Nylon fibres and possible wastewater sourcesThe study reported that microplastics were present in 60 of the 63 snakes examined, equivalent to approximately 95% of the sample. The researchers identified 390 microplastic particles across the specimens. Fibres accounted for 96.9% of the particles identified, while fragments and films made up the remaining 3.1%. The polymer analysis identified nylon and polypropylene, with nylon accounting for 80% and polypropylene for 20% of the particles analysed. These proportions should not be interpreted as representing all microplastic particles recovered from the 63 snakes. These proportions should not be interpreted as representing all microplastic particles recovered from the 63 snakes.Because fibres predominated and nylon was identified, the authors suggested domestic laundry wastewater as a possible source of the microplastics. However, the study did not trace the particles to a specific discharge point or establish their origin. The proposed source should therefore be treated as a hypothesis rather than a confirmed explanation.Age and regional differences remain uncertainThe researchers examined age-related and regional differences in microplastic ingestion within the Arabian Gulf coral reef sea snake (Hydrophis lapemoides), rather than across all 63 snakes in the study. Of the 39 specimens of this species, 34 came from the Arabian Gulf and 5 from the Gulf of Oman. Exposure was higher among younger snakes and among those from the Arabian Gulf, but neither pattern was statistically significant. The small number of Gulf of Oman specimens limits the conclusions that can be drawn from the regional comparison.What the findings establish, and what remains unknownThe findings have important limitations. The sample consisted of stranded animals rather than a random sample of the wider living sea-snake population, and the study was geographically restricted to Sharjah. The uneven numbers of specimens across the 6 species also limit how far the findings can be generalised.Detecting microplastics in the gastrointestinal tracts does not establish that ingestion caused illness or death. Further research involving larger samples and wider geographic coverage would help establish whether the observed age and regional patterns persist. Studies linking particles to potential pollution sources and investigating biological effects would also be needed to determine the broader implications for sea snakes. The central finding is that microplastics were detected in 60 of 63 stranded sea snakes representing 6 species along Sharjah’s coasts. The study identifies domestic laundry wastewater as a possible source, but the precise origin and effects of the particles remain unresolved.

articles.title: Jackie the bald eagle's mysterious cause of death revealed
articles.summary: The new report sheds light on what ultimately led to the death of the Big Bear Lake, California, bald eagle who was beloved by millions around the globe.
articles.body:
Jackie , the beloved California bald eagle whose life was watched via live video feeds by millions around the world, died of complications resulting from avian influenza, according to a newly released necropsy report.

"Jackie's necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," Steve Kubiski, director of disease investigations for the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, said in a statement Wednesday, Oct. 14. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis."

The newly released report sheds light on the mysterious illness that veterinarians struggled to treat throughout the summer. The Big Bear Lake, California, bald eagle's life was livestreamed on YouTube, leading to her becoming an object of global fascination and to her hometown becoming practically synonymous with America's iconic bird.

She died in August after a weeks-long fight with an illness that confounded the eagle's doctors. Efforts to save Jackie saw her hospitalized and placed under anesthesia for veterinarians to perform what many hoped would be a life-saving blood transfusion. Veterinary pathologists at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance performed the necropsy.

According to the report released by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the avian flu left Jackie with a severe stomach ulcer that led to ongoing blood loss and ultimately a deadly bacterial infection.

"Together, the findings showed that Jackie was suffering from multiple severe and interconnected disease processes that had been developing over time and ultimately led to her decline and death," the California Department of Fish and Wildlife said of the report.

The state agency said that HPAI is a highly infectious disease that has been circulating in wild bird populations throughout the United States. Eagles and other raptors are believed to contract the disease through contact with infected birds or by eating infected prey. Waterfowl and shorebirds are natural carriers of the viruses.

Jackie was hatched in 2012, the first eaglet to do so in Big Bear Valley, USA TODAY previously reported . Her parents, Ricky and Lucy, became the first known adult eagles who decided to stay in Big Bear Valley, which until then had only been a part-time winter destination for the species. Big Bear Lake is about an hour northeast of San Bernardino in Southern California. She lived in Big Bear Valley in the San Bernardino National Forest.

Tender moments show bald eagle couple Jackie and Shadow in the wild

She became a viral sensation a few years later when U.S. Forest Service employee Sandy Steers got the idea to install a webcam 120 feet off the forest floor to broadcast her life.

Jackie found her first romance in 2017 when she mated with an eagle named Mr. B. The couple's eggs hatched in 2018, and while one of the eaglets died after a 24-hour rainstorm, the other, named Stormy, survived and left Big Bear that summer.

Her second mate, Shadow, remains in Big Bear, state authorities said. California wildlife officials said that there is nothing to indicate he or their eaglets, Sandy and Luna, are sick.

"The story of the Big Bear bald eagle reflects the powerful connection people feel to these iconic birds," said wildlife agency Director Meghan Hertel. "We're grateful to everyone who cared for her and worked to support her well-being. Understanding the results of these tests is an important part of learning from this case and can help inform the care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife in the future."

articles.title: A Wyoming ranch dog found a black-footed ferret in 1981 after the species was presumed extinct; 45 years later, none were found at the site
articles.summary: In September 1981, a barking dog interrupted the sleep of a Wyoming cattle rancher and his wife, and a morning discovery became one of the most remarkable
articles.body: In September 1981, a barking dog interrupted the sleep of a Wyoming cattle rancher and his wife, and a morning discovery became one of the most remarkable stories in wildlife conservation. What the dog had dragged home looked like a masked animal, yet it belonged to a species that officials had already written off as extinct. Within hours, a local taxidermist was making a phone call that would bring biologists to a ranch. This article follows the dog's discovery, the hidden colony it revealed, the disease crisis that nearly erased the species, and the recovery that brought the animals home.The night a ranch dog named Shep woke John Hogg and his wife and left a strange carcass at the ranchAn account from the Fort Collins Museum of Discovery, says that at about three o'clock in the morning on September 26, 1981, cattle rancher John Hogg and his wife, Lucille, were woken by their dog, Shep, barking just outside the bedroom window. Assuming Shep had tangled with a porcupine again, they went back to sleep. The next morning, Hogg found what the dog had actually caught, the carcass of a small animal with a black mask, black feet and a black-tipped tail, its back broken. Lucille thought it might be worth having mounted, so the couple drove it into Meeteetse to the local taxidermist. He took one look at the animal, fell quiet and said he needed to make a phone call.Why a Meeteetse taxidermist dropped everything to call Wyoming officials about a black-footed ferretThat phone call changed everything. Driggs reports that the animal was a black-footed ferret, a species whose official history seemed to leave no room for doubt: the last wild population had vanished by the mid-1970s, and the last ferret in captivity died in 1979. By every official account, the species was extinct. The taxidermist's call reached Wyoming wildlife officials, and biologists soon arrived at the Hogg ranch to investigate. The significance was enormous, because a single carcass suggested that a living population might still exist somewhere nearby. Driggs describes the moment as the start of a chain of events that would either save a species or confirm its extinction, and the biologists lost very little time in finding out which.How biologists located 120 to 130 black-footed ferrets on two ranches after years of failed searchesSurveys, trapping and radio tracking turned up a small colony living quietly on the Hogg property and the neighbouring Pitchfork Ranch, Driggs reports: about 120 to 130 ferrets, the last known wild population on the planet. The article stresses that the colony was a long shot nobody had managed to find on purpose. In the late 1970s, Wyoming newspapers had run stories and advertisements asking ranchers to report any sightings of the species, and none ever turned up. As Driggs puts it, it took a dog's late-night encounter to do what years of searching could not. The discovery placed two working ranches at the centre of the species' fate and gave biologists a living population to watch, at a time when the animal was officially considered gone.How distemper and plague in 1985 pushed the black-footed ferret to just its last 18 breeding animalsBiologists spent the next few years watching the colony, but Driggs reports that in the summer of 1985 disease tore through it. Canine distemper and plague struck the ferrets and their main food source, prairie dogs, at the same time, and the population crashed. Wildlife managers brought six ferrets into captivity that fall to start a breeding program, yet all six caught distemper and died within weeks, according to Wyoming Game and Fish. Bob Oakleaf, a former Wyoming Game and Fish biologist, later told the agency that there was a "big debate" about what to do with the animals once they were found. By February 1987, officials had removed every ferret they could find from the wild: seven males and 11 females, 18 animals in total, the species' entire breeding population.How 18 ferrets rebuilt a species, returned in 2016, and why none were found at Meeteetse this summerThose 18 ferrets became the foundation of a captive breeding program, Driggs reports, and reintroductions eventually reached 29 sites across eight states, Canada and Mexico. According to the Wyoming Game and Fish Department, in 2016, wildlife officials released 35 captive-bred ferrets onto the Hogg and Pitchfork ranches, yet the Associated Press reported on October 13, 2026, that late-August surveys of 4,000 to 5,000 acres detected none. Plague flared in 2018 and 2019, leaving one confirmed animal in 2020, and plague returned in 2023 after releases helped the group recover. Andy Gygli, a Wyoming Game and Fish biologist, told WyoFile that drought has also hurt prairie dogs, the ferrets' main prey, so he diverted 10 captive-raised ferrets to Shirley Basin. Allen Hogg told WyoFile, "I'm not saying all hope is lost."

articles.title: US biotech firm completes 95% of dodo's genome and identifies gene-editing targets; could the extinct bird come alive again through its closest living relative, the Nicobar pigeon?
articles.summary: Among all the animals and birds that have gone extinct, the dodo remains unforgettable, not due to some special characteristic, but because, before its
articles.body: Among all the animals and birds that have gone extinct, the dodo remains unforgettable, not due to some special characteristic, but because, before its human-driven extinction, many thought that nature was inexhaustible and none of god's creations would ever disappear. It proved that human activity had the capacity to wipe out an entire species. More than 300 years after the bird disappeared from the face of Earth, an American biotech company claims it is making progress in its goal of resurrecting the famous flightless bird, as per a Reuters report.Dallas-based Colossal Biosciences said on Wednesday that it has used a newly developed AI platform to identify genetic changes that may be responsible for the dodo's distinctive craniofacial traits as its scientists pursue gene-editing targets to bring back the lost species. Colossal is planning to perform gene-editing to bring the dodo traits into the cells of one of its closest living relatives, the Nicobar pigeon. Native to some Southeast Asian islands, the Nicobar pigeon is known for its shimmering green and copper feathers but unlike the dodo, it can fly.Ancient DNA is always broken into small pieces, so no ancient genome is perfectly complete, including that of the dodo. It made use of a new AI platform called GenoMorph. "The challenge was that scientists only have one complete dodo genome, making it difficult to distinguish the genetic differences that made the dodo unique from ordinary genetic variation. GenoMorph effectively acts as a 'treasure map' for the dodo genome, narrowing hundreds of thousands of possible genetic changes into the targets most likely to explain its iconic beak and facial structure," Lamm said.Beth ​Shapiro, Colossal's chief science officer, said GenoMorph finds ​likely gene-editing targets for species with very ⁠little surviving DNA. Normally scientists compare many genomes from one species to find the genes behind a trait, but this is not possible with the dodo, Shapiro said.The company said it is in its final stages of analysis of the dodo genome, now filled to 95%. It also said it has made an advance that should shorten the time needed to test whether a genetic edit produces the desired trait. However, it did not announce any timeframe for hatching a dodo.Colossal says it is dedicated towards "de-extinction", which involves resurrecting vanished species. In 2025, it said it has genetically engineered the dire wolf by editing the genes of the grey wolf, the extinct Ice Age predator's closest living relative, to add dire wolf traits.Including the dodo and dire wolf, Colossal has four other species on its de-extinction list: the woolly mammoth; the thylacine, also called the Tasmanian tiger; the bluebuck antelope; and the moa, a large flightless bird."The dodo is the world's best-known symbol of extinction caused by people. It disappeared within decades of humans arriving on Mauritius, largely because of the introduction of invasive species like rats and other animals they brought. Bringing it back shows extinction doesn't have to be permanent," Ben Lamm, Colossal's CEO and co-founder, told Reuters. "The big hurdles ahead are proving which genetic changes really matter, making many of those edits in a bird and passing them to the next generation, and preparing a safe home for dodos on Mauritius," Lamm said.The dodo was a flightless, ground-nesting bird about 3 feet tall and weighing 50 pounds. Having never encountered humans, dodos were fearless of the people who reached Mauritius in the 16th century. Due to consistent pressure from invasive species and human hunting, the last living dodo was seen in 1662. It ‌has remained ⁠alive in popular culture, including in Lewis Carroll's book "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland."
