articles.title: Mars forms a 1,800-kilometre cloud nearly twice the length of the UK near a giant volcano every morning, and scientists think it may form ice without dust
articles.summary: Every morning during spring and summer in Mars’s southern hemisphere, a long white cloud appears downwind of the giant volcano Arsia Mons.
articles.body: Every morning during spring and summer in Mars’s southern hemisphere, a long white cloud appears downwind of the giant volcano Arsia Mons. The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud, or AMEC, can stretch up to 1,800 kilometres before fading, a length the European Space Agency (ESA) compares with nearly twice the length of the UK. The cycle repeats each morning for several months. For years, scientists struggled to reproduce the cloud’s distinctive features in computer simulations. Now, a study published in Nature Geoscience suggests an unexpected explanation: the cloud may form through a process in which water vapour turns directly into ice without needing pre-existing particles such as dust. The researchers used observations from the European Space Agency’s Mars Express spacecraft alongside a meteorological model. Their results strongly suggest that this process, known as homogeneous ice nucleation, occurs on Mars, although the mechanism has not been directly observed.Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud on Mars: how a 1,800-kilometre water ice cloud formsThe AMEC is a water ice cloud that develops downwind of Arsia Mons, a giant Martian volcano that ESA describes as about 20 kilometres high. ESA reports that the cloud can reach 1,800 kilometres in length. It reappears in the morning during the southern hemisphere’s spring and summer, then dissipates as the day progresses. The cloud is an example of an orographic cloud, which forms when air flows over elevated terrain. The simulations indicate that air flowing over Arsia Mons produces a strong atmospheric wave. As moist air rises rapidly, it cools and its relative humidity increases, creating conditions that may allow ice to form. The combination of the volcano’s height and Mars’s thin atmosphere creates conditions that the model identifies as suitable for the cloud’s formation.Earlier simulations using conventional cloud-formation processes struggled to reproduce the AMEC’s observed characteristics. Under the usual explanation, water vapour forms ice on pre-existing particles suspended in the atmosphere. This process is called heterogeneous nucleation. On Mars, airborne dust is thought to provide some of these surfaces. The new study, Homogeneous ice nucleation from water vapour suggested by elongated clouds on Mars, published on October 7, 2026, proposes that the AMEC may form without this requirement. Its explanation depends on the extreme atmospheric conditions produced as air rises beside Arsia Mons.Homogeneous ice nucleation on Mars: how water vapour can form ice without dustLead author Jorge Hernández-Bernal, affiliated with the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique and Sorbonne Université in Paris, and his colleagues investigated whether homogeneous ice nucleation could explain the cloud. In this process, ice particles form directly from water vapour without relying on pre-existing particles to initiate their formation. The distinction matters because homogeneous nucleation requires exceptionally high levels of supersaturation, when the amount of water vapour exceeds the equilibrium amount under the prevailing conditions. It has been considered theoretically possible in the upper atmospheres of Earth and Venus, but has not previously been observed in nature in a planetary atmosphere.The researchers incorporated homogeneous ice nucleation into a meteorological model of Mars. With this process included, the simulations reproduced key characteristics of the AMEC that had proved difficult to reproduce using conventional cloud microphysics alone. The results strongly suggest that the cloud’s formation involves homogeneous nucleation. The findings do not mean that scientists directly watched individual ice crystals form without dust. Instead, the proposed mechanism explains the cloud’s observed behaviour within a model. The authors also report that some features of the simulated cloud do not match the observations exactly. The study therefore offers evidence for a process that atmospheric scientists have generally considered unlikely under real planetary conditions. It also suggests that the extreme humidity needed for homogeneous ice nucleation may occur in Mars’s atmosphere, even though such conditions had not previously been observed there.Mars Express observations of the Arsia Mons cloud and implications for other planetsThe observations used in the research came from ESA’s Mars Express spacecraft, which has monitored the cloud over several years. Mars Express has observed the recurring cloud over several years. In September 2018, its Visual Monitoring Camera began a detailed series of observations that helped scientists document the cloud’s daily evolution. For the study, the researchers used data from 3 Mars Express instruments: the Visual Monitoring Camera, the High Resolution Stereo Camera and OMEGA, the Visible and Infrared Mineralogical Mapping Spectrometer. Together, these instruments provide observations that help researchers examine the cloud’s appearance and its relationship with the Martian atmosphere and surface.Mars Express can observe the planet during the morning hours when the cloud is present. ESA’s ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter also has an orbit that allows observations during these hours. The timing matters because the cloud develops and fades over a relatively short period. ESA Mars Express project scientist Colin Wilson said the mission could track changes in the cloud over timescales of hours, helping scientists study short-lived atmospheric phenomena. The new work builds on years of observations by using them to test a possible explanation for how the cloud forms.The implications could extend beyond Mars. If homogeneous ice nucleation can occur under real atmospheric conditions on the planet, scientists may need to consider the process when modelling clouds in other environments. The findings may also prompt researchers to reconsider cloud-formation processes in some Earth and planetary atmospheres. However, the study does not establish that homogeneous ice nucleation occurs in those environments. The research was supported by the French space agency CNES and the European Research Council. For now, the key result is that a model incorporating homogeneous ice nucleation can reproduce important features of one of Mars’s most striking clouds. Further work will be needed to test the proposed mechanism and determine how broadly it applies.

articles.title: Russia says Ukraine resumes attacks on oil refineries
articles.summary: Ukraine’s president earlier said Kyiv was ‘done’ with energy ceasefire and that strikes on Russian oil refineries would resume.
articles.body:
Russia says Ukraine has targeted an oil refinery in Ryazan, about 180 kilometres (110 miles) south of Moscow, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was “done” with an energy ceasefire unilaterally announced by United States President Donald Trump over the weekend.

“The Kyiv regime attempted a large-scale attack on an oil refinery in Ryazan,” Moscow’s defence ministry said in a statement on Thursday, adding that a “fire broke out after drone debris fell onto the refinery site.”

Ukraine’s president earlier told the British newspaper the Financial Times that strikes on Russian oil refineries would resume, and accused the US of weakening Ukraine’s position on the battlefield by allegedly withdrawing crucial intelligence sharing.

Trump on Sunday unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” that was not publicly confirmed, and Moscow continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Ukraine said it suspended attacks on Russian energy sites for several days after Trump’s announcement.

The US has pressured Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian refineries, claiming that a suspension of attacks and a deal to purchase 1.8 million tonnes of diesel from Russia would help reduce soaring fuel prices .

“This politically is not simple [in America], because everybody will want to ask how it can be when some people are surviving, fighting, dying – and you make . . . business with the guys with such aggression,” Zelenskyy told the FT.

Zelenskyy also alleged that Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s satellite internet service was restricted, potentially leaving it more vulnerable to Russian attacks. The Ukrainian armed forces use SpaceX’s military-grade Starshield system for offensive and defensive operations.

In a post on X on Wednesday evening, SpaceX owner Elon Musk said that only the US military and Trump had the authority to limit Starshield’s usage and speed for clients.

In a separate post, he called for Zelenskyy to “go” as Ukraine’s leader.

“And so the slaughter continues,” Musk wrote in a separate post on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.”

Ukraine is heavily dependent on Western military aid in its fight against Russia, particularly from the US and Germany. However, Kyiv’s relations with Washington have been strained in recent weeks, with Trump calling on Saturday for Zelenskyy to be replaced.

Against this backdrop of tensions, Zelenskyy said he would be willing to pause strikes on Russian energy sites again, but only if the US supplied Ukraine with crucial Patriot interceptors.

Zelenskyy is due to meet European leaders in Brussels on Thursday as he pushes for tougher sanctions on Moscow and faster delivery of support from the European Union.

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten has called on EU leaders to “step up” their game to ensure Ukraine wins the war against Russia.

The EU has already pledged $50 billion in support for Ukraine next year. However, the sum falls far short of the $175 billion Kyiv plans to spend on its defences next year.

Trump has denied that the US has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

articles.title: A 13-year-old Indian-American student invented a system to fight ocean acidification; she won America's Top Young Scientist title and a $25,000 prize, while two other Indian-origin girls took the remaining top honours
articles.summary: At 13, Raji Doshi is already thinking about a problem that scientists around the world are racing to solve: what happens when the oceans absorb too much
articles.body: At 13, Raji Doshi is already thinking about a problem that scientists around the world are racing to solve: what happens when the oceans absorb too much carbon dioxide? The Connecticut student has developed a potential way to tackle ocean acidification using algae and a naturally occurring mineral, earning her the top prize at one of America’s leading science competitions for middle school students, states an online report by 3BL media.A young scientist takes the top spotAccording to 3BL media, an eighth grader from Farmington, Connecticut, Doshi was named the 2026 winner of the 3M Young Scientist Challenge, a national competition organised by 3M and Discovery Education. The title came with a $25,000 prize and the distinction of being named America’s Top Young Scientist, the report adds.Doshi emerged from a field of 10 finalists aged between 11 and 14, each tasked with identifying a real-world problem and developing a scientific solution. The finalists spent the summer refining their projects with the guidance of 3M scientists before presenting their work at 3M’s global headquarters in St. Paul, Minnesota, on October 12 and 13.Turning algae into a climate solutionDoshi’s project focuses on ocean acidification, a consequence of rising carbon dioxide levels that can threaten marine ecosystems and organisms that depend on calcium carbonate to build shells and structures, the report informs.Her system, called ALKACORE, combines macroalgae cultivation with aragonite, a natural form of calcium carbonate. The idea is to increase the alkalinity of seawater while helping remove carbon dioxide, potentially creating a durable and relatively low-cost approach to reducing coastal acidification.Her research went beyond lab work. Doshi investigated how aragonite affects algal growth and carbon dioxide using carbonate chemistry. She also developed a Michaelis-Menten computational model to identify an optimal aragonite dose, an important step towards exploring how such a system could eventually be adapted for practical use, the report adds.The inspiration was also deeply personal. Her interest in seashells led her to notice the damage that increasing ocean acidity can cause to shell-forming marine life, turning a childhood curiosity into a scientific investigation, explains the 3BL media report.Two more Indian-origin finalists shineDoshi was not the only Indian-origin student to make her mark in this year's competition. Aaisha Asif, a seventh grader from Sarasota, Florida, and Sharvi Mahajan, a ninth grader from San Diego, California, claimed second and third place respectively. Both runners-up received $1,000 prizes, giving the competition a strong showing from young Indian-origin innovators.Where curiosity can leadNow in its 19th year, the 3M Young Scientist Challenge is designed to give middle school students an opportunity to turn curiosity into practical scientific work. Each finalist is paired with a 3M scientist for one-on-one mentoring, helping students develop their ideas, test solutions and communicate their findings. The competition has also become a launchpad for young innovators, with previous winners going on to pursue patents, launch nonprofits, deliver TED Talks and earn places on the Forbes 30 Under 30 list.Image Courtesy: 3BL Media

articles.title: What is Starshield, and who limited Ukraine’s access to it?
articles.summary: Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service, to fight Russia.
articles.body:
Ukraine’s military Starshield satellite connection has been restored, a Ukrainian Ministry of Defence source says, just days after the United States reportedly restricted the service.

The Reuters news agency, quoting a source, reported that Kyiv is still seeking clarifications from Starshield’s parent company, SpaceX, as to why its service was disrupted between Tuesday and Wednesday.

Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s internet service, Starlink, to provide intelligence amid its war with Russia.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has denied the company’s involvement and suggested only the US government could have disrupted it, despite President Donald Trump’s insistence that Washington is still sharing intelligence with Kyiv.

Starshield is a sister service to Starlink, an array of 11,000 satellites placed by SpaceX into Earth’s low orbit to provide high-speed internet connectivity even in remote areas.

Starshield, launched in 2022 and provided to the US government, is designed for military use as it allows for deeper encryption to process sensitive information. SpaceX says it is primarily used by US defence agencies and other “government partners”.

Ukraine’s military relies on Starshield, especially to guide its drones, on which it relies heavily to attack Russia.

What happened to Ukraine’s access to Starshield?

On Tuesday, Ukrainian defence officials said they had lost access to important satellite-based communications and that the disruptions had affected military missions. This came in the wake of heavy Russian strikes, which hit the country with more than 100 drones and five ballistic missiles, for which Ukraine said it had received no prior warning.

“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X. “Regarding this strike, unfortunately, there was no warning from partners.”

Serhiy Beskrestnov, a defence adviser to Zelenskyy, posted on Telegram that SpaceX had also “implemented a speed limit” on Starlink terminals, capping internet speeds at 100mph (160km/h).

That meant any drones or missiles flying at more than 100mph lost their guidance connection.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” he said, adding that this was clearly “related to the current political situation”.

Officials said the restrictions also reduced capabilities for front-line logistics, reconnaissance and relaying signals.

On Wednesday, Musk denied any involvement in the incident, insisting that the service is “controlled by the US government”.

Responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said the speed limits were being lifted and demanded unrestricted internet speed, Musk wrote, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.”

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said, referring to the US president.

Musk further clarified that Starlink is for “civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company” – an apparent attempt to differentiate it from Starshield, which Kyiv also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations.

Last year, Starlink cut off access for Russian troops who were covertly using the service on the battlefront in Ukraine.

The SpaceX boss has shown an active interest in the Russia-Ukraine war since it began, but has not been particularly favourable towards Kyiv. In 2022 – just after Russia invaded Ukraine – he proposed a “peace plan” under which Kyiv would end its claim to Russia-occupied Crimea and would drop hopes for joining NATO. Zelenskyy criticised Musk’s comments, and tensions between the two have remained.

On Sunday, the billionaire, who is also the CEO of Tesla and owns X, said Zelenskyy “has gone too far”, in a response to Trump’s comments that the Ukrainian president should leave office.

On Wednesday, Musk appeared to blame Zelenskyy for deaths in the war. “And so the slaughter continues,” he wrote on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.”

Does Ukraine blame the US for restricting intelligence?

Ukrainian officials have complained that the country received no warning in advance of Russian ballistic missile strikes on Tuesday and Wednesday. Usually, the US provides crucial early-warning alerts that allow Kyiv to issue evacuation orders.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday that US military officials had earlier warned Kyiv that Washington would block intelligence unless attacks on Russian energy infrastructure stop.

The Ukrainian leader added that he did not accept suggestions that the Starshield incident could have been a glitch. “It was not a technical problem; it was the will,” he said.

Why might the US restrict intelligence from Ukraine?

Tensions between Kyiv and Washington have been building since Trump took office last year over a host of issues, including weapons transfers and the US’s increasing closeness to Russia.

In recent weeks, Washington has pressured Ukraine to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries to allow more oil into global markets. In particular, Trump has sought to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel facilities for the rising price of the fuel globally ahead of November midterm elections.

Trump said last week he had agreed to a deal with President Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel stocks into the US and global markets, despite existing sanctions on Russian oil.

Zelenskyy criticised the move and said it would embolden Putin.

Over the weekend, Trump unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, apparently without consulting Zelenskyy, who told reporters the deal was “news to me”. Russia also did not confirm it. Angered, Trump called for Ukraine to replace its president and blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure for global energy disruptions.

Ukraine said it had, in fact, refrained from attacking Russian refineries and would continue to do so if Russia did the same. However, Russian strikes have continued. On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure had caused blackouts affecting 600,000 people.

“We’re done,” the Ukrainian president said in the FT interview, confirming that Kyiv had subsequently resumed attacking Russia’s oil infrastructure.

articles.summary: A sandwich Gabriella Rothberg was making for her father when she was 15 led to an unusual question: Could a tomato be made to taste like meat?
articles.body: A sandwich Gabriella Rothberg was making for her father when she was 15 led to an unusual question: Could a tomato be made to taste like meat? Two years later, the 17-year-old student from Miami is listed as a co-inventor on a US patent for genetically engineered tomatoes designed to produce heme, an iron-containing molecule associated with the flavour of meat.Gabriella, a senior at Ransom Everglades School in Coconut Grove, worked on the project with her father, biotechnology entrepreneur Jonathan Rothberg. The two are named as inventors on US Patent No. 12,668,806, issued in June this year. According to the report by Biscayne Bay Beacon, the patent has been assigned to Impossible Vines Inc.The idea behind the project is to develop tomatoes that produce heme, which contributes to the characteristic flavour of meat. Gabriella hopes the technology could eventually make vegetables taste more like meat without requiring them to be processed into conventional plant-based meat substitutes.However, the project is still experimental. The genetically engineered tomatoes have not undergone taste testing or entered commercial production. Researchers have also not established whether they can deliver the intended flavour or nutritional benefits. The patent protects the described technology but does not establish that the tomatoes are ready for consumption.How a sandwich idea became a biotechnology projectGabriella began thinking about the project at 15 while preparing a sandwich for her father. She wondered whether it would be possible to change the flavour of a vegetable itself rather than process vegetables into products designed to resemble meat. That question eventually developed into a biotechnology project called Impossible Vines.Speaking to Miami New Times, Gabriella explained what she hoped the technology could achieve. "So you'll bite into a tomato, and it'll taste like a hamburger," she said.To explore the idea, Gabriella worked with Maddison Marshall, a doctoral candidate at the University of Miami. Together, they used a bacterium called Agrobacterium to introduce genetic material into tomato plant cells.Agrobacterium is used in plant genetic engineering because it can transfer genetic material into plant cells. In this project, the researchers used it to work towards developing tomatoes capable of producing heme.Heme is an iron-containing molecule associated with the flavour of meat. The researchers' aim is to enable tomato plants to produce it through genetic modification.The patent also describes methods for changing other characteristics of plants, including their lycopene content and seed production. Lycopene is a naturally occurring pigment that gives tomatoes their red colour.Researchers faced problems growing the modified plantsGabriella and Marshall also faced difficulties during the early stages of their research. For several months, the plants did not develop as expected. The researchers then consulted scientists at the University of Miami to understand what was preventing growth.They eventually discovered that the vitamin concentration in the growth medium was incorrect. The growth medium is the material used to provide plant cells with the nutrients needed to develop under laboratory conditions. After adjusting the formula, the researchers began seeing plant growth within weeks.Gabriella also reported using artificial intelligence during different stages of the project. She used AI tools to help design genetic constructs, prepare patent materials and develop a business plan.Gabriella comes from a family of biotechnology researchersGabriella's interest in science developed in a family with a background in biotechnology and medical research. Her father, Jonathan Rothberg, is a biotechnology entrepreneur who helped pioneer next-generation DNA sequencing. He had received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation from former US President Barack Obama in 2016. Her mother, Bonnie Gould Rothberg, is a cancer researcher at the University of Miami.Gabriella says that scientific discussions were common at home. Family conversations often included subjects such as evolution, astronomy and physics. The patent also lists Gabriella alongside her father as an inventor.Could the tomatoes also help address iron deficiency?Beyond developing tomatoes with a meat-like flavour, Gabriella hopes the technology could eventually help improve access to dietary iron.She has suggested that vegetables containing additional iron could be useful in regions where meat is expensive or difficult to obtain.Gabriella also identified pregnant women in developing countries as one group that could potentially benefit from iron-enriched vegetables.

articles.title: A 150-million-year-old bird fossil has unusually small wings and dinosaur-like teeth; the discovery challenges the idea that the earliest birds were all built primarily for flight
articles.summary: For millions of years, the evolution of flight has been the story of birds.
articles.body: For millions of years, the evolution of flight has been the story of birds. But a remarkable fossil from southeastern China suggests some of the earliest birds may have preferred to keep their feet on the ground. The new species lived about 150 million years ago, and had surprisingly small wings for a bird, sharp teeth, and a powerful claw that would have made it well suited for life as a terrestrial hunter, according to an online report by Reuters.A bird that may have preferred to runThe crow-sized species, named Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, lived during the Jurassic Period and is among the earliest-known birds, Reuters reported. The find gives us a new look at how feathered dinosaurs gave rise to the birds we see today, suggesting that early members of the bird lineage might have experimented with a variety of ways to move around and survive.The fossil, which is almost complete, was discovered in Fujian Province in south-eastern China. The animal is thought to have weighed about 800 grams, or 1.8 pounds. It had fully developed wings but the size of the wings compared to the size of the body suggests it might not have been able to engage in prolonged powerful flight.Yuezhuornis probably depended on running for much of its activity, flying only when it had to. Its proportions are similar to those of modern ground-dwelling birds such as pheasants, giving clues as to how it might have moved through its prehistoric habitat, the report states.An odd mix of bird and dinosaurWhat is particularly interesting about the fossil is the combination of anatomical features it exhibits. Its skeleton had some very bird-like parts, like its slender skull bones and pelvis. Other features were far more similar to those of a predatory dinosaur.Its jaws were crammed with closely packed, serrated teeth, a characteristic more usually associated with carnivorous dinosaurs than modern birds. A long, bony tail added to its dinosaurian appearance, the report says.The animal also had a sickle-shaped claw on its flexible second toe, like the deadly claws of meat-eating dinosaurs such as Velociraptor and Deinonychus. This adaptation may have allowed it to catch or subdue prey on the ground, potentially putting it into competition with small predatory dinosaurs, the report continues.Its wings were especially telling. The researchers found it was about a third shorter than its legs, a stark contrast to the more balanced proportions of the early birds adapted for flight.Rethinking the origin of flightArchaeopteryx, discovered in Europe, has been a central figure in discussions of early bird evolution for decades. It also had bird-like and dinosaur-like traits, from roughly the same time period. But the better proportioned wings suggest a larger capacity for flight than those of Yuezhuornis.The new find raises questions about whether early birds took one evolutionary route. Researchers think the two species may have shared a common ancestor earlier in the Jurassic period, but Yuezhuornis could also be its own evolutionary experiment.Its limb proportions were most similar to those of birds adapted for terrestrial life, further supporting the terrestrial lifestyle hypothesis in comparison to 377 extant bird species.An ever-changing story still in the makingThe fossil, the report said, doesn't answer exactly how flight evolved, but it challenges the assumption that the earliest birds were shaped largely by the demands of flying. Others may have developed other survival strategies. Others may have descended from flying ancestors and become more ground-dependent.Yuezhuornis is a reminder to scientists examining the origins of birds that evolution rarely takes a neat, predictable course. The earliest birds weren't all variations on a flying theme. Some may have been clumsy fliers, efficient runners and fearsome hunters, showing a much more diverse prehistoric world than previously imagined.Images Courtesy: istock

articles.title: Egyptian farmer tilling the land discovered 28-foot statue of biblical pharaoh who enslaved Israelis, allegedly challenged Moses in Bible
articles.summary: In Egypt's Behbeit El Hagar, located in Gharbia province, a farmer truly dug deep.
articles.body: In Egypt's Behbeit El Hagar, located in Gharbia province, a farmer truly dug deep. While tilling the land in front of his home, the man discovered a royal statue of Ramases II, the pharaoh who allegedly challenged Moses in the Bible. According to a report by the New York Post, the farmer flagged the local antiquities official, after which a team working for the Supreme Council of Antiquities launched an excavation, according to Heritage Daily.The treasure trove reportedly revealed an over 5-foot-tall head of Ramses II that's depicted sporting the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt. As per the size of the noggin, archaeologists projected that the entire statue measured over 27 feet tall, including the base. Researchers also recovered part of the statue’s back pillar, which bears an inscription containing one of the pharaoh’s royal names.Another, smaller royal statue that measured just under eight feet tall was also unearthed. Also uncovered was a 4-foot-high block of pink granite containing fragments of hieroglyphic inscriptions proclaiming the pharaoh "Nesu Beti", meaning King of Upper and Lower Egypt and "Sa Ra," meaning Son of Ra.While the figure’s legs and base were missing, its face was clearly visible and bordered by nemes, the striped royal headdress worn by ancient Egyptian pharaohs. These characteristics, along with the fact that the visage resembled the other statue, suggested that it was also a Ramses II facsimile.Ramses II, born in 1303 BC, is widely considered one of the most influential and powerful Egyptian kings of Egypt's New Kingdom era (1570 to circa 1069 BC). The ruler is also popularly linked to the story of Moses in the biblical Book of Exodus, even though the holy text doesn’t mention him by name. In that account, the ruler enslaves the Israelites and defies Moses, incurring God's wrath.Sherif Fathy, Egypt’s Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, said that the findings will hopefully contribute to a greater understanding of this region of the Nile Delta, which was a political, cultural and economic stronghold in ancient Egypt. The officials hope that further studies will help shed light on the statues and the architectural evolution of the repository during the epoch in question. Fathy also praised the homeowner for promptly reporting the stone rather than attempting to remove or keep it, highlighting the role ordinary citizens can play in protecting Egypt’s cultural heritage for future generations.Archaeologists are continuing to excavate the site and examine the relationship between the two statues, the inscribed granite block and their surroundings.

articles.title: Scientists surveyed people who went on shark tours in Hawaii and found they were 40% more likely to engage in shark conservation than they would have been without the experience
articles.summary: Shark populations around the world are in rapid decline, facing mounting threats from human activities.
articles.body: Shark populations around the world are in rapid decline, facing mounting threats from human activities. With a third of shark species threatened with extinction, new research suggests that shark ecotourism could help turn the tide by encouraging people to take lasting action to protect them.New research from the University of Sydney found that people who participate in shark ecotourism are more likely to take action to protect sharks, including making donations, signing petitions and speaking up online, than those who do not. This is the first study to demonstrate that shark ecotourism can inspire a lasting commitment to conservation, with participants more likely to take action.Alongside increasingly positive media coverage and online attitudes towards sharks, the findings suggest that this tourism offers more than economic benefits. It could help protect declining shark populations. The findings are published in the journal Ocean Sustainability.How shark tourism can lead to conservationOver the past 50 years, shark populations have declined by 71%. A third of shark species are now threatened with extinction. At the same time, shark ecotourism is growing, with more than 500,000 people estimated to take part in activities involving sharks and rays each year. At least 20 countries, including the Bahamas, Australia, Hawaii, South Africa and Pacific nations such as Fiji, Palau and French Polynesia, offer such activities.The research, led by PhD candidate Carmen Dobszewicz of the University of Sydney’s Faculty of Science, examined how ecotourism benefits sharks. Dobszewicz is based in the Social Dynamics and Environmental Change Lab within the School of Life and Environmental Sciences.Her team worked with two groups in Hawaii. The first comprised tourists on a shark ecotourism tour off Oʻahu. They snorkelled or free-dived with sharks while a marine biologist surveyed the animals and explained why they matter. The second group comprised members of the public surveyed on Waikīkī Beach. Both groups answered questions about shark conservation on the day of the tour and again two years later.How shark tours change attitudesParticipants were asked whether they had engaged in shark conservation activities after the ecotour. The study revealed that, two years after their tour, participants were about 40% more likely to engage in shark conservation behaviour than would have been expected had they not taken part.In both groups, conservation activities increased over the two years. The rise was considerably larger among the tour group. Among these participants, the biggest increases were in posting on social media, signing petitions, making donations and advocating for legislation.The researchers noted that responsibly conducted shark encounters can lead to long-term conservation efforts.“Our findings suggest responsible tour operators can be a much-needed boon to efforts to halt the rapid decline in shark populations and help shift widely held misconceptions about sharks,” Dobszewicz said.“Supplementing the underwater experience with educational information on the role sharks play in the ecosystem, the threats they face, and what can be done to mitigate these threats leaves tourists with a better understanding of the precarious state of shark populations and what we can do to try to rebuild them.”The research builds on the Social Dynamics and Environmental Change Lab’s ongoing work on the relationships between people and nature that underpin a sustainable future.“Conservation ultimately depends on people. When we build or strengthen meaningful connections between people and the natural world, we create the conditions for lasting change, and that is essential for a sustainable future,” senior author Associate Professor Michele Barnes said.

articles.title: Withings now charges $100 per year to sync your data to other apps
articles.summary: Withings now requires new users to subscribe to its Withings Plus service to sync health data from its smart scales and watches to third-party apps.
articles.body: If you’re a new user of Withings’ fitness-tracking smartwatches or smart scales and want to sync and access your health data through third party apps like Apple Health or Google Health it’s now going to cost you. According to a discussion on Withings’ support forums spotted by MacRumors, new Withings accounts created from October 13th, 2026, and onwards will require a Withings Plus subscription to use the “automatic sync to third-party apps” feature. The subscription costs $9.95 per month or $99.50 per year but Withings’ devices come with a free one month trial that includes the option to sync their data to third-party apps. When the trial is over the syncing is paused but the data in those apps isn’t deleted. Existing users who already have a Withings account created on or before October 12th, 2026, will continue to have access to automatic third-party app syncing for free, according to official comments shared by a member of Withings’ support team. And because the feature is tied to an existing users’ account and not a specific device, the third-party syncing will continue to be available without a subscription if they buy and register new watches, scales, or other Withings hardware.
